Our research involves creating a Monte Carlo model to understand the concentration of cosmic ray alphas and protons trapped around Earth, specifically in low-altitude orbits. This phenomenon, known as Charge Radiation of Alphas and Neutral particles at Debris, releases secondary particles when cosmic rays interact with the Earth's magnetic field. These trapped particles can determine the composition of cosmic rays and their energy spectrum. Since the rates of these radiation are extremely low, they are difficult to measure in low-altitude orbits, making simulation essential to validating detector data and understanding the phenomenon. Our Monte Carlo model successfully replicates the characteristics of CRAND radiation in this orbital range, and we found that the rates of radiation in low-altitude orbits are dominated by protons. This model will allow us to accurately interpret experimental results and understand radiation in this region.

A comprehensive neural network structure for deep graph learning has been proposed, incorporating a dynamic global skeleton with a pyramid-like framework and an adaptive network with link reconfiguration. This design tackles the challenges of graph size, complexity, and coordination through a two-phase approach: initially developing a coarse-skeleton for data reduction and down sampling, and then iterating over local topology links to incorporate node and edge attributes, thereby enhancing the network's ability to learn end-to-end representations. In order to enhance the learning process, a detailed training procedure involving node and edge cross-view learning, attribute projection, and refinement is presented. This framework's potential is demonstrated through its application in three distinct graph learning tasks: node classification, link prediction, and graph representation learning. Comprehensive numerical evaluations of the framework's performance are presented, along with empirical studies of the deGNN's performance characteristics.

The objective of differential privacy is to safeguard users' data while sharing completed matrices containing missing values with third-party providers. This paper presents an innovative solution by applying the Huber method to privately complete large matrices in an efficient manner. The proposed method combines the Lasso technique to first generalize the matrix's data points, and subsequently applies the Huber method to recover the original matrix's structure under private conditions. Compared to existing methods such as the Alternating Least Squares approach and several other iterative algorithms, the Huber-Lasso method exhibits superior performance in matrix completion, while also being one of the first to achieve private results using this approach.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust, differentiating it from the widely-used FM model with a clear separation of observational evidence supporting distinct dust components. The enhanced model includes small grains originating from star formations, as well as larger particles inherited from these events, referred to as astrodust. By introducing a straightforward method for determining dust optical depth based on subvisual extinctions, we can extract total dust mass without the need for complex optical models. The mass thus calculated is then used to predict the Al and Si abundances. The empirical relationship between the average optical depth of extinction at 550nm and the optical depth at 90nm allows us to determine the ratio of albedo to optical depth, from data of polarization measurements. By applying this approach, we can determine the albedo at 550nm. The emission from interstellar dust, described by the DDA model, includes two components, one originating from the Al203 and SiO2 crystals and the other from the carbonaceous particles. The emission from these two components has distinct ratios of flux, accounting for the wavelength dependence of the emission. The combined emission from these components matches the 21-185μm data published in the NASA Astrophysics Data System, a database that contains thermal emission data from interstellar sources. The model also includes an algorithm to determine the extinction, emission, and polarization coefficients from total dust mass and albedo at 550nm. The specific mechanisms behind the formation of planets around low-mass stars and small planetary bodies remain poorly understood.  In this study, researchers used extensive observations of the low-mass star CIDA 1 with the VLT to investigate its planetary system.  Notably, the team discovered signs of a massive planet, similar to Jupiter, at a distance of 1.04 astronomical units from the star.  They found evidence that this planet cleared its surroundings, leaving behind an area devoid of small dust particles and where the orbital debris cloud was not influenced by external factors.  Furthermore, the team observed signs of the planet's influence on the surrounding material, manifesting as gaps and changes in the material's distribution, which matched theoretical expectations for the effects of a planet of its size and location.  Ultimately, the findings imply that planetary systems, even those around low-mass stars, can be influenced by massive planets, which can explain the data for CIDA 1.

The Lights Out problem, originally known by this name on Nokia 221, is a well-known electronic game that receives limited attention in the scientific community. In this study, we explore the most taps required to solve this game in n keys with certain constraints. Assuming key durability varies from 1 to infinity, we also consider situations where keys have the same level of durability. In designing our solutions, we draw inspiration from the binary counting system. For keys with the same level of durability, our algorithm uses a variation of our general solution suited to their conditions. These results are verified through practical examples and analysis of their efficiencies. We conclude by examining extensions to our problem where multiple electronic games are combined.

This paper presents a novel, advanced image segmentation model, which builds upon the breakthrough image restoration model \emph{ExpDecayGammaGV} by Ling et al. [2017]. To enhance image segmentation, we incorporate graded covariate information and apply the weighted convex generalized Kullback-Levlier divergence to the proposed model. The model's performance is demonstrated through extensive experiments using various real-world image datasets.

The Galois-connection based abstract interpretation framework involves the application of fixed-point computations over a complete lattice to derive approximate semantic value, relying on forward or backward simulations to define operators between related abstract domains. However, standard fixed-point algorithms necessitate the monotonocity of the operator, limiting simulations to Galois connections with convex abstract domains in Galois pair and triple connections. To address this limitation, we have developed a fixed-point computation method for non-convex domains using alternating iterations, combining forward and backward simulations to derive approximate value. In contrast to existing techniques, our approach can handle non-convex domains using Galois pair and triple connections, offering greater flexibility with domain configurations. We have theoretically validated the soundness and termination of our proposed algorithm for accurate value derivation. Furthermore, our approach has been experimentally validated on a well-known technique for spatio-temporal reasoning problem solving.

The properties of phonons play a crucial role in determining the performance of electronic devices based on oxides. Recent experiments have shed light on the topological characteristics of phonons in ABO3 perovskite compounds, revealing a unique property known as "negative refractiveity". This phenomenon occurs when the phonon velocity across a specific direction reaches its maximum, resembling the topological characteristics of electronic bands. A new theoretical framework based on the Bloch theorem is introduced to analyze this phenomenon, relying on the phonon momentum rather than frequency. The phonon "Poincare band" is a result of this new framework, allowing for the visualization of phonon properties across the momentum-space. A comparison between experimental results and theoretical predictions highlights the role of optical modes in describing topological phonons, indicating that the 180-degree rotational symmetry in ABO3 perovskite compounds is responsible for the "Poincare band" structure. The theoretical framework established in this study can be applied to other quantum systems with rotational symmetries, potentially leading to the design of new phonon-based devices.

We present an efficient algorithm for identifying anomalies in metric spaces, one data point at a time. Building on the 'nearest-neighbor classification' concept, this approach leverages graph theory to significantly accelerate both learning and outlier detection processes. Unlike traditional classification methods, our technique excels at handling complex, high-dimensional data sets, achieving computational efficiency similar to that of nearest-neighbor classifiers. As a result, our algorithm can quickly train and deploy on complex, large data sets within a short time frame. We validate the performance and scalability of our approach using a range of synthetic and real-world data sets, comparing it favorably with established outlier detection methods.

The theoretical basis for motion-induced stimulation and electromagnetic radiation from an atom facing a moving mirror has been established using quantum electrodynamics. It's been observed that when an atom is placed in front of a stationary mirror and oscillates, it gives off radiation by stimulating the vacuum. On the other hand, when a stationary atom is placed in front of a moving mirror, both radiation and stimulation occur. Moreover, radiation from the atom is given off not just during the atom-mirror interaction, but also after the atom has passed the mirror, and its frequency does not depend on how the mirror was accelerated. It's also been noted that radiation from the atom is given off in a pattern that does not depend on its position, and when calculated, the atom's radiation is found to be no more than expected classical radiation. It's also been noted that radiation from the atom is given off in a pattern that does not depend on its position, and is influenced by the atom's dipole moment. On the other hand, a moving atom that collides with a stationary mirror produces radiation that depends on the atom's initial and final positions, and the atom's acceleration, and is influenced by the atom's multipole moments. It's also been noted that radiation from the atom is given off in a pattern that does not just depend on its velocity, but also the mirror's curvature and the atom's dipole moment, and when calculated, the atom's radiation is found to be no more than expected classical radiation

Graph representation learning has garnered significant interest, with a standard fair representation assumption that distributes similar representations across connected nodes equally being somewhat rigid. To address this, we introduce a new concept of community fairness with adaptability in mind, allowing us to specify how similar representations should be distributed over the graph in a more flexible way. By defining a neighborhood with a clear start and end point, we can accurately identify both the graph's structure and the groups within it using our novel objective function. Numerical experiments confirm that our proposed fairness assumption offers a more practical and effective choice than existing methods for a wide range of tasks, including those where labels are unavailable.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  The resulting approximations demonstrate a comparable level of accuracy.  Supporting Matlab codes for both methods are provided in the appendices.

This study introduces a new search for supersymmetry, focusing on low-energy scenarios where superpartcles were not directly detected but left behind kinetic energy. The investigation utilized data collected from high-energy proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically a 2016-2018 data set with an aggregate of 138 inverse femtobarns. The search targeted final stages characterized by high-energy jets and considerable kinetic energy, with an emphasis on complex jet arrangements. The selection process, informed by machine learning, prioritized events featuring significant kinetic energy and those supported by multivariate statistical indicators. To enhance the detection process, the researchers corrected for uncertainty factors and calculated the probability of occurrence. The analysis then excluded multiple possible scenarios where extra particles were present in final stages. The researchers further compared their findings with theoretical predictions of supersymmetry scenarios, specifically focusing on natural supersymmetry scenarios where mass imbalances occurred near 400-450 GeV in final stages.

We developed a novel financial bubble diagnostic model based on a single equation, analyzing an asset price's difference as it deviates from an anticipated value. The scenario considers consumers exhibiting rational, expectational behavior with an uncertain timeline for reevaluating their predictions. The equation employs a generalized variance, adapted from a novel fractional $F$-distribution that mimics the characteristics of the standard $F$-distribution as its parameters approach infinity. A simulation study revealed that, in cases of finite parameters, the proposed fractional $F$-distribution still effectively models critical properties as asymptotes. Furthermore, a numerical investigation demonstrated that, in cases of limited data samples, the suggested generalized $F$-distribution maintains excellent fit accuracy compared to the standard $F$-distribution. Finally, an empirical analysis was conducted to test the effectiveness of the proposed diagnostic model in detecting financial bubbles within two actual stock market datasets.

This paper introduces a novel method for employing the path integral approach to solve the driven harmonic oscillator utilizing the discrete Gaussian Monte Carlo technique. By integrating this method with the Markov chain Monte Carlo method, it enables the efficient calculation of the oscillator's absorption and emission rates. These rates are calculated by evaluating a specific time integral that appears in the formula for the driven oscillator's transmission and absorption coefficients. While the time integral's relation to the oscillator's properties is well-established, it remains an understudied aspect in the broader path integral method. To address this, we employed the Gaussian action approximation and represented the associated integrand as a product of two terms. By rotating the integration variables 90 degrees, we were able to derive an exact representation of the time integral in terms of Gaussian integrals, which enables the efficient calculation of the oscillator's transmission and absorption coefficients at both high and low temperatures. Furthermore, through the numerical calculations, it is demonstrated that this method can accurately reproduce known results in the single-phonon regime, thereby validating the method's effectiveness.

Recent research has shown significant interest in improving recommender systems through data from customer reviews. The basic review-based approach using topic representation overlooks the nuanced sentiment expressed by customers. This paper proposes a novel model called SIFN, which dynamically combines both review content and sentiment to produce more accurate results. The model's conditional CNN module captures the diverse sentiment patterns, while its dual attention mechanism effectively integrates review content and position-sensitive sentiment features. The model's interactive fusion layer then combines the review and item embeddings in accordance with their mutual similarities. The model's output is further enhanced through a softmax function. The model's performance was demonstrated through experiments on the Yelp and Amazon review datasets, which showcased its superiority over competing baselines.

Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by a severe data scarcity problem. In an effort to create more CS training resources, this research explores the effectiveness of data augmentation through lexical substitution in CS text. Conducting experiments on Arabic-English CS has shown that using all possible lexical substitutions leads to improved results, and employing sampling techniques further enhances performance. Notably, using all possible substitutions is beneficial despite the excessively large search space, and this advantage persists across various vocabulary sizes. Moreover, we found that constrained lexical substitution is not necessary and that an unrestricted approach is sufficient. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/nphoenix/LASAR-CS.

Our research shows that any infinite collection of surface homeomorphisms whose uniform topological conjugacy classes do not collapse is never compact in the sense of the Roelcke topology, thereby answering a question that was posed by Gura and Pustyl'nikov. This consequence can also be applied to the set of infinite string subshifts homeomorphic to the M\"{o}bius band subshift to yield an alternative proof of a finding by Ostantnikov. Furthermore, our findings extend to infinite collections of surface homeomorphisms with non-constant height under the condition that they are uniformly topologically conjugate to a collection of pseudo-Anosov homeomorphisms.

By applying a generalized lambda deformation to the standard SO(4) module, we construct integrable membrane operators within the three-dimensional space. These membrane operators' characteristics are defined by a system of algebraic equations derived from a generalized deformation of the SO(4) group. We then obtain, as a specific case, membrane operators under the generalized lambda deformation of the Euclidean group E(3), specifically when the lambda parameter equals 2. To complete our analysis, we demonstrate that the membrane operators' characteristics form an associative algebra under convolution and recover, as a specific case, the deformation of the Euclidean algebra e(3), specifically when the lambda parameter equals 2.

The measurement of tetrahedral mesh quality is typically based on the worst-case 
error of all its tetrahedra, which can be inaccurate as it represents only one 
element despite the significant role of other, higher quality tetrahedra in the 
mesh. To assess the overall quality of a hexahedral mesh, we propose a new, 
efficient method that estimates the average and distribution of all hexahedral 
tetrahedra in the mesh, based on the worst-case error of the worst 1%, 5%, 15%, 
50%, and all tetrahedra. To achieve this, we developed two efficient mesh 
unwrapping methods: a precise but slow, floating point-based approach, and a 
faster, coarser approximation that produces close to 56 tetrahedra per hexahedron. 
We evaluated our approach using three large, practical-sized meshes, each paired 
with an existing tetrahedralization method, and found that our estimated 95th 
percentile and 99th percentile errors of 0.03% and 0.33% can be as much as 66% and 
79% higher than the errors obtained using the worst tetrahedra, respectively, in 
one of the tested scenarios, indicating the utility of our proposed approach for 
assessing the overall quality of a hexahedral mesh.

The task of relation extraction, which involves extracting relationships between entities, has been studied for over two decades in natural language processing. Despite the numerous methods and models developed for relation extraction, these approaches often rely on limited, annotated data, which can lead to poor performance on new relationships. In contrast, knowledge graph link prediction, which tries to fill in missing links in existing graphs, uses large, unannotated data sets. By leveraging these data sets, we can generate synthetic training data that can improve relation extraction. In this paper, we propose a novel technique that uses knowledge graph link prediction to create more relevant synthetic relation extraction samples. Our approach, which adapts the Transformer model to balance the two tasks, achieves state-of-the-art results on dataset benchmark evaluations.

A novel approach to developing high-fidelity models of power conversion systems starts with characterizing their conversion processes, which cannot be captured by conventional lumped models. To overcome this limitation, analytical inverter models with embedded lookup tables are proposed. By incorporating lookup tables into conventional analytical models (e.g., average-and-peaking models), the resulting embedded models can provide accurate system-level simulations, including non-linear behavior. The feasibility of this methodology is demonstrated through a case study using MATLAB's Pspice and the Curve Fitting Toolbox, which facilitates model development by translating non-linear lookup table data into rational function form. The success of this case study underscores the potential to utilize this methodology for developing precise models of power conversion systems.

Many deep reinforcement learning algorithms face challenges due to complicity issues in non-continuous action and state spaces. Although employing continuity assumptions can facilitate the analysis and development of these algorithms, providing rigorous continuity proofs can be complicated. This research introduces new continuity results that can accommodate a broad range of algorithms, including those using continuous and discrete action spaces, by employing a metric space framework. These findings not only relax the requirements for differentiability but also generalize continuity results, providing solid analytical foundations for a wide range of reinforcement learning methods.

The animacy organization refers to a fundamental property where living entities are categorically distinguished from non-living objects. Previous studies mainly investigated this concept using face and body perception expertise, which are both closely linked to animacy. However, it remains unclear whether these are unique cases or if a broader range of concepts, such as animals versus objects, also conform to animacy principles. Utilizing behavioral experiments and functional magnetic resonance scanning, we found that concepts like animals versus objects indeed conform to animacy principles and activated the same temporal brain network, including the fusiform area, inferior temporal lobe, and posterior occipital complex. Notably, individual differences in activity to animal stimuli in this network predicted behavioral performance in an animacy task. Since object expertise typically activates a more posterior and lateral occipital-inferotemporal network, we suggest that animacy principles may reflect two distinct mechanisms: a more general differentiation process activated by anim objects and a more complex differentiation process required by non-object concepts like animals.

In the context of multibody dynamics and fluid dynamics, where traditional finite difference and finite element methods are commonly employed, these methods can generate nonsmoothing results at the boundaries when applied to individual component simulations. Consequently, merging such individual unit results can lead to loss of structural integrity. This paper introduces an innovative algorithm that helps preserve the inherent structure of the system by utilizing a convex optimization framework. By leveraging many of the same numerical techniques used to construct the discretization scheme, this convex method generates smooth boundary conditions compatible with structural requirements. When combined, these conditions and traditional finite element results form a seamless and consistent framework for multibody dynamics and fluid dynamics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our convex optimization algorithm by applying it to various problems, including 1- and 2-dimensional systems.

We analyzed type-C Comptonization time-lags from a near-optimal 2.915 s episode of quasi-periodic fluctuations (QPFs) in the 2-10 keV MAXI J1535-571 data observed by Insight-HXMT, with an epistemic uncertainty range of $6.72-8.34 \mu$Hz, corresponding to a 26-30 s QPF period. By separating the light curve into three energy bands (3-5, 5-8, and 8-20 keV) and performing time-lag analysis from the first two, we found that the corona in the inner accretion flow of the source transitioned from thermal to stratified behavior. This was indicated by a time-lag pattern that changed from positive to negative as the QPFs developed, with an interlude where the middle energy band light curve remained relatively flat or had an uncertain positive value. We speculate that this behavior can be attributed to a geometrically complex and possibly two-dimensional inner corona that is dynamically changing, suggesting that the outer stratum of the corona forms after the onset of the QPFs, potentially as a result of an inner electrostatic instability.

In the field of robot learning, many social robotics applications rely on interaction between robots. Most existing methods focus on teaching individual robots to behave, ignoring the importance of social interaction. This lack of understanding leads to robots behaving erratically when interacting with each other. To address this, this paper introduces a novel approach that leverages the concepts of transfer learning and intrinsic reward during agent training. This method enables robots to accurately respond to their partner's actions by introducing a unique reward signal while leveraging experience transfer. Experiments conducted in a simple task demonstrate the efficacy of this method in teaching robots to interact and achieve a joint goal.

We introduce MatNet, a comprehensive, worldwide material database consisting of 12,304 unique material samples, each featuring four associated images that incorporate diverse lighting conditions, including reflection, transparency, and an anisotropic finish. MatNet is designed to facilitate rapid, worldwide material identification using real-time rendering of materials via computer graphics engines, utilizing a variety of image pairs generated from physically-based material descriptions. Our experimental results demonstrate that a combination of a ResNet(50)-based feature extractor and a supervised contrastive learning approach on a small subset of data yields exceptional performance, particularly when compared to traditional methods. Moreover, we experiment with cross-domain material identification and successfully apply it to our dataset, allowing for accurate material identification in unseen domains. Our extensive MatNet dataset and corresponding code are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/phonk21/MatNet.

Two equivalent definitions of Lie 2-algebras are examined, along with their
corresponding linear versions known as Lie 2-algebras without a 2-algebra structure.
The survey reveals some recurring themes and challenges arising from these two
definitions, attempts to provide extensive relevant examples and offers a few
openly acknowledged unsolved problems. The majority of the work focuses on
(2,1)-algebras defined by two multilinear operators of degree 2 and 1, as this
definition is seen as the most natural and versatile.

Our research proposes LoFTR, a novel vision alignment method that employs only
pose estimation without relying on explicit feature detection. By treating image
registration as a masked self-attention task, LoFTR leverages the strengths of the
Transformer model to facilitate local matching across images. Since it doesn't
require detecting distinct features, LoFTR excels at cross-domain, cross-season,
and real-world challenges involving significant changes in appearance. On the NTIRE
2019 challenge dataset, LoFTR surpasses the state-of-the-art with a PSNR of 34.83,
an improvement of 1.28 points over the previous best method. The code for LoFTR is
available at https://github.com/acme-ai/loftr.

The conversion of spectroscopic lines into magnetic field strength values relies on the 1D local line formation model. However, the model's validity is often compromised due to unrealistic minimum gas pressure and temperature values. Such inaccuracies manifest as lateral (2D) effects that can be quantified by the first derivative of the model's minimum gas pressure and temperature boundaries. By employing the finite element method, these derivatives can be calculated and their integration would normally result in an apparent change in minimum gas pressure and temperature, thereby biasing magnetic field strength and inclination measurements. This study has developed an automated test to detect bias in these measurements by analyzing the change in gas pressure and temperature, with higher values indicating more significant lateral effects and resulting bias. This test allows for the assessment of bias using the same data as the inversion process, with the choice of selecting the apparent change in gas pressure and temperature. The results show that roughly 18% of test cases exhibit noticeable bias, with more than half the cases requiring an adjusted inversion technique. This study has also adapted an existing inversion technique to mitigate bias by modeling the apparent change in gas pressure and temperature. The results show that implementing this modification can significantly reduce bias, with up to 90% of test cases exhibiting minimal bias, thereby improving the accuracy of magnetic field strength and inclination measurements. Moreover, the study has found that applying the modified inversion technique with the auto-bias technique can reveal features such as polar regions, regions of strong magnetic field, and equatorial regions

This research paper presents a novel approach to Demand Side Management (DSM) through an instant-labeled game that simplifies user interactions with the energy consumption scheduler. To overcome the difficulties of an instant-labeled game, an aggregative game is designed to facilitate simultaneous decision-making by users, resulting in a joint optimal strategy that equals the Nash equilibrium. Furthermore, the paper outlines an efficient algorithm for determining the Nash equilibrium of the aggregative game under the premise that each user's demand is perfectly divisible by 5. Finally, numerical evaluations were conducted to illustrate the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed method in achieving joint optimal results and reducing energy consumption peaks.

Utilizing the Rastall theory of gravity, which incorporates a divergence-free symmetric tensor, we establish the equations of motion for charged black strings. We investigate the thermal properties of these black strings as well as their horizons' behavior, and as a result, we analyze the impact of gravity in the Rastall theory on Hawking radiation.

The convergence rate of the ergodic theorem for weakly ergodic transformations can be defined using the operator norm of the limit measure's finite range factors or by the decay rate of a weighted spectral measure. We show that a convergence rate based on a weighted spectral measure directly corresponds to the ergodicity level, specifically weak ergodicity. Since weak ergodicity doesn't directly relate to strong ergodicity, we investigate metrics for space of measures and show that a convergence rate based on a weighted spectral measure is sensitive to these differences, whereas the ergodicity level is not. We provide numerical examples to support our findings.

The data released by the Gaia mission, including spectra from the BP and RP spectrometers, offer a vast amount of information, mainly used to determine the photometric properties of the mission's target stars. However, this information contains valuable details about the stars' elemental composition, which can be easily accessed using relatively simple techniques. In order to uncover these details, a method using neural networks to analyze the stars' spectra was developed, allowing for the detection of metal-poor stars with temperatures between 4000K and 6000K at a rate of 83%. Additionally, this method can also determine carbon levels with a high degree of accuracy and detect stars with low metalicitiy using more complex neural networks.

The period between mid-June to mid-July is known as "blaze season" in Australia, a time when the entire country experiences severe heat waves, resulting in significant potential for widespread wildfires. Throughout this critical period, precise forecasting of temperature and precipitation predictions are vital in reducing the risk of future outbreaks. However, accurate precipitation prediction poses a challenge, influenced by multiple factors such as large-scale atmospheric conditions, surface interactions, and the dynamics of precipitation itself, making it a complex issue. This research aims to investigate factors contributing to the severity of wildfires during this specific period and explore the potential for predicting precipitation in the next 10 days. Notably, our findings show that by considering only a two-week perspective, we can identify factors contributing to the severity of wildfires, without being able to do so when looking at longer time frames. This is consistent with the idea that the onset of precipitation beyond two weeks is less likely. This is further substantiated by the fact that the geometric mean of precipitation probabilities beyond two weeks becomes arbitrarily small.

We've conducted a thorough examination of the variability in definitions and operationalizations of morphological complexity, focusing on English and singular plural forms. Our research reveals that, despite being widely used in linguistic data preparation, the underlying criteria for evaluating complexity are often unclear or ambiguous. We've identified five distinct criteria: coverage, consistency, uniqueness, simplicity and representativeness, and length. By assessing these criteria using statistical methods, such as principal component analysis and clustering, we found that English morphological complexity can be categorized into three distinct types. Our findings are compared to existing approaches, and we suggest new methodologies for understanding these three forms of complexity. Furthermore, we discuss limitations and potential applications of these results and suggest that broader discussions and collaborations among NLP practitioners would lead to more informed decisions on handling complexity in data preparation.

Researchers at Harvard discovered extremely small gravitational lenses within the galaxy clusters 1E2214-66 and HydraAA0227-4302, which exhibit the shortest known values for the constant Newton's constant for gravity. To fully understand these lensing effects, models of the universe must incorporate either self-interacting dark matter or irregular densities of dark matter. Either of these options could potentially lower the expected mass of small gravitational lenses, which could explain the observed phenomenon if Newton's constant for gravity has different values in different galaxy clusters. Furthermore, these results have significant implications for the theory of non-Abelian gauge symmetries, as they suggest that dark matter might be part of a non-Abelian gauge theory of matter. To investigate this idea, our research used both semi-analytical and numerical methods to simulate galaxies within the universe, which revealed that the average density of dark matter in galaxies decreases with increasing distance from the center of the galaxy. Our models also showed that the weight of dark matter in galaxies decreases with increasing distance from the center of the galaxy, which cannot be explained by the mass of visible matter in galaxies. Any theory of the universe that relies on self-interacting dark matter must also incorporate a mass function that allows for the transfer of momentum between different particles of dark matter, which cannot be a feature of the universe that exists independently. Dynamic model simplification is successfully implemented for a series of real-world datasets. The process, which is represented as a step-by-step workflow, utilizes partial least squares for handling missing and incomplete data, followed by an information-theoretic approach to feature selection. The workflow's efficiency is demonstrated through its application on datasets from the field of healthcare and on a financial dataset from the UML classification system. The implementation of the model simplification workflow is provided through the RStudio environment using the 'filterSimplify' package.

This paper proposes the autonomous analysis (AA) of M-ar-K-Fast, a variant of the
arithmetic hidden Markov model (AHMM). The model's analytical nature enables
component-based AA, allowing for automated model feature extraction without
need for initial parameter specification. The derived model components possess
intuitive interpretations similar to those of the traditional multinomial
components, which is a crucial characteristic of the model. The article introduces
the theory and practical implementation of the AA method, accompanied by a
proof-of-concept example of using red pine tree height data to illustrate the
model's capabilities.

When catastrophic events like floods, wildfires, and earthquakes occur, people often share critical safety information on social media in emergency situations. However, extracting relevant data from vast amounts of real-time social media posts can be challenging due to the abundance of irrelevant information generated during crises. To address this problem, we have developed an incident detection system utilizing geotagged social media posts and temporal information. Our approach consists of two key components: (1) identifying trending locations that may be affected by incidents, and (2) aggregating text data from identified locations to detect incidents in real-time. The performance of our system was evaluated using recall, precision, and F1 score metrics across various platforms, including Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram. To optimize processing efficiency, our system incorporates a data filtering step before applying algorithms to analyze spatial and temporal data. Our experimental results demonstrate that our system achieves an average F1 score of 0.1599, outperforming traditional incident detection methods that rely solely on text analysis.

We examine the solution $u$ of the elliptic problem $-\Delta u = \mu$ in $R^N$ with $u \in H^1(R^N)$, $u>0$, given that $\mu$ has compact support. Considering the case where $R^N$ is divided into two parts by a $C^{1, \alpha}$ surface $S$, and with a signed measure $\mu$ concentrated on $S$, we establish the continuous dependence of the problem's solution with respect to small changes in the surface's geometry. Furthermore, this investigation leads to the development of a new elliptic obstacle problem.

This research focuses on discovering compounds rich in cobalt by utilizing advanced computational methods called evolutionary search algorithms, which enable an extensive exploration of the phase diagram of the Yttrium-Cobalt-Boron system. Based on previous studies, the system's phase diagram is relatively unknown, and there is limited information available. Therefore, to initiate the search, various starting conditions are applied using the evolutionary algorithm, which identifies three cobalt-rich compounds: YCo$_{16}$B$_{22}$, YCo$_{22}$B$_{14}$, and Y$_{2}$Co$_{16}$B$_{26}$. These compounds stabilize within the system and exhibit cobalt abundances of around 50-60%, largely confirming predictions made using another computational method known as first-principles calculations. Notably, the cobalt-rich compounds stabilize through the fusion of small cobalt-boron clusters rather than the reduction of cobalt ions. Additionally, the cobalt-rich compounds exhibit properties such as high conductivity, high magnetism, and interesting magnetic structures with several magnetic domains. These properties may be beneficial for applications in materials such as transparent conductors and permanent magnets, and further studies could potentially customize these compounds to meet the requirements of cobalt-rich compounds with tailored properties.

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the predominant approach. advertisers place bids on newly published ads in a rapid sequence as ads switch frequently, creating numerous challenges for decision-making. Most existing studies assume a specific cost function. However, the primary objective of an advertiser is to maximize the total ad impressions (e.g., reductions in conversions) while keeping expenses within a set budget. This paper tackles a new challenge called ad impression risk management, which involves developing a bidding strategy to minimize the cost of ad impressions while adapting to the fluctuations in prices. To achieve this goal, the paper introduces an adaptive bidding strategy based on the principle of submodularity and a polynomial-time method to minimize the cost of ad impressions while keeping expenses within a set budget. By leveraging the idea of impression budget allocation and simplifying the problem, the paper reduces the computational complexity and develops an efficient algorithm to tackle the problem. Finally, the paper presents the results of the hypothesis testing to verify its effectiveness through the comparison with the benchmark solution, which is known to have a computational complexity of exponential scale.

Non-classical behavior in quantum information processing often manifests as odd Schrödinger cat states and quantum entanglement, which are inherently linked to each other. Recent studies have provided lower bounds on the amount of entanglement that can be generated through quantum steering, thereby indicating the relationship between entanglement and non-local steering. This paper examines the relationship between quantum steering and Wigner negativity, which is a localized resource, to conclude that Wigner negativity is not a sufficient indicator for quantum steering capability. Moreover, we investigate how local operations and classical communications (LOCC) can mitigate Wigner negativity and demonstrate that Wigner negativity can serve as a measure of quantum steering strength. The dependence of Wigner negativity on the quantum state dimension is also studied in the context of Wigner Negativity's resource theory.

This paper focuses on the secure evaluation method for quantum key distribution (QKD) experiments that utilize non-uniform random seeds within the privacy amplification process. By adopting this approach, we reexamine the key rates of a QKD protocol known as the long-distance hybrid quantum key distribution protocol utilizing single photons from multiple thermal sources. Comparative analyses are performed between secure evaluation methods, specifically those using uniform and non-uniform random seeds. Notably, our results show that uniform and non-uniform random seeds exhibit comparable efficiency in promoting secure key rates. Furthermore, we investigate the potential consequences of non-uniform randomness by assessing its impact on the entire quantum key distribution process, not just privacy amplification. This investigation reveals that non-uniform random seeds can extend the practical application range of the considered QKD protocol, thereby contributing to the optimization of practical outcomes. Ultimately, our analysis contributes to the optimization of practical outcomes in QKD experiments.

This research paper focuses on examining a specific type of curve in a semi-metric space, known as a timelike Bertrand curve. An initial investigation reveals that non-timelike Bertrand curves are dense and dense regular. Further, a definition for a Bertrand component is established, and it's shown that a timelike Bertrand curve can have at most one Bertrand component. Additionally, a key result indicates that a timelike Bertrand curve is either null or spacelike if its geodesic curvature is zero, and it's shown that a timelike Bertrand curve's direction field can never be tangent to the curve.

We examine the statistical characteristics of Feller processes, specifically in relation to the coalescent times, and demonstrate how these are affected by the associated sampling distribution. Our investigation includes a discussion on the compatibility of these processes with the Fourier series-based criteria. Moreover, we derive explicit expressions for the coalescent times and sampling distribution in the context of Lambda and Lambda Lambda models. These expressions enable us to compare the associated sampling distributions, and identify instances where they match. Finally, we analyze the properties of the resulting models, paying particular attention to their demographic histories, population sizes, and the likelihood of having a recent common ancestor. These characteristics are exemplified through a focus on models with zero, two, and five ancestral lineages at present time.

In this work, we develop a new method to analyze the scattering of multi-photon states in waveguide QED systems using an innovative diagrammatic approach. Unlike traditional methods, our approach seamlessly handles an infinite number of internal degrees of freedom in the system's Hamiltonian, which describes the interaction between light and matter. By employing a specific parameterization, we are able to accurately diagrammatically represent the physical Hamiltonian and its equivalent in the scattering basis. This breakthrough enables us to systematically derive a systematic effective theory for multi-photon states in waveguide QED systems. Furthermore, we apply our approach to examine the scattering of two photons in systems consisting of multiple qubits, which leads to the derivation of consistent effective couplings between photons, thereby confirming the conservation of lattice symmetry.

In the context of a non-relativistic dark matter model with a potential, we examine how accelerated dark matter influences interactions involving spins. Specifically, we investigate the implications for direct and indirect detection methods. For direct detection, our analysis shows that dark matter with accelerated motion at densities below a certain threshold can be detected by experiments sensitive to spin-dependent interactions. This result has significant implications for the interpretation of direct detection data. For indirect detection, we found that a sum over final states in the loop, particularly a sum over spin-dependent $f \rightarrow \bar{f} g$ transitions, has a significant impact on the calculation of indirect detection rates. This contribution is particularly important when the initial and final states have non-trivial spins. For both direct and indirect detection, our analysis focused on a specific model in which the interaction between dark matter and standard model particles is mediated by a tensor boson. For indirect detection, our results show that accelerated dark matter can impact loop-induced processes such as indirect detection via loop processes, particularly for momentum-dependent terms. Finally, our analysis shows that accelerated motion can be most effectively probed by measuring the velocity distribution of Galactic dark matter particles using Earth's center of mass frame.
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

This paper presents a novel approach to monotone likelihood ratio metric (MLRM) non-coherent detection for continuous phase modulation (CPM) signals, which has been widely used due to its simplicity in various applications, including binary phase shift keying (BPSK) and binary differential phase shift keying (BDPSK). Their inherent similarities have gone largely unnoticed in the literature, leading to a potential unified analysis. We compare the delay of a conventional non-coherent differential CPM (CPM) detector with that of a conventional CPM detector and demonstrate, both theoretically and practically, that the former experiences a significant increase in delay. A constructive method to mitigate this issue is also discussed. We verify the validity of our findings through simulations involving different CPM signals.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via ranking to embed desired properties into target functions. However, existing ranking algorithms face efficiency hurdles, particularly when dealing with large numbers of tasks, leading to prolonged processing times. To overcome this limitation, our approach proposes a faster and more reliable method, leveraging visually aided techniques to rank tasks and thereby significantly reducing processing times. Our method utilizes hierarchical clustering, aided by visual support, to efficiently generate a large number of task rankings. Experimental evaluation across multiple domains demonstrates the efficacy and speed of our proposed ranking algorithm.

To investigate the nucleon's distribution of quark and diquark, a two-quark model is employed, enabling the determination of quark distribution functions within nucleons and diquarks in noncommutative space-time. Utilizing the Lattice QCD proton structure functions obtained from Barras, Ostermann, and Schäfer's work and incorporating Gao and Lu's results on the noncommutative parameters $ \theta_1$ and $ \theta_2$, this model examines the nucleon's quark distribution functions derived from lattice simulations. Additionally, the model calculates the nucleon's electromagnetic form factors, considers noncommutative corrections to nucleon structure functions, and explores the implications for nucleon parton distributions in the presence of space-time noncommutativity.

This study delves into the characteristics of kagome and triangular lattice implementations of the Taubin code, a variant of the toric code designed to exhibit geometric defect behaviors. The research involves a systematic reduction of these models' non-abelian degeneracies through the introduction of a commuting Hamiltonian, whose inclusion Triviality reduces the previously non-abelian eight-fold degeneracy to a two-fold abelian one. In both systems, the derived Hamiltonian displays a geometric structure, mirroring the network's topology, and the underlying reason for the degeneracy reduction, as well as its relationship to the encountering of multiple entropic regularities, is analyzed. Furthermore, the analysis extends to a more general class of boundary Hamiltonians and explores their impact on the entropy regularity's critical exponent.

We investigate the eigenvalue spectrum of a zero-row-finite-rank complex perturbation to a real Gau\ss{}ian band matrix. This analysis alignes with the statistical-physics "universal class" consisting of real band matrices with zero-rank infinitesimally small perturbations. Our computational method yields an approximation that effectively predicts the eigenvalue spectrum. Our results demonstrate that the eigenvalue spectrum behaves like a non-linear sigma model depending on the perturbation's matrix properties. Moreover, the eigenvalues converge towards the embedded eigenvalues of the unperturbed matrix. Our findings also validate that the spectrum's lower bound lies within the range defined by the absolute value of the perturbation matrix's largest eigenvalue and the square root of its trace.

Recent advancements in dialogue systems have been achieved through large-scale pre-trained language models. These models, like ELMO and BERT, are trained using unsupervised and supervised data to capture the underlying grammar and semantic meaning in language. However, dialogue understanding requires both the ability to analyze syntax and semantics, as well as the correct integration of these elements in the context of a conversation. In an effort to build a dialogue model with superior understanding capabilities, we suggest modifying the existing BERT model to include a context-aware module for dialogue processing. This enhanced model can be trained on both a syntax-based mask task and a semantics-based mask task without the need for labeled data. Our analysis reveals that this syntax-and-semantics aware model significantly improves performance in tasks such as answering questions, classifying text, and predicting the tone of dialogue in the Twitter dataset and the MultiWOZ dataset.

To develop more effective machine learning models for real-world scenarios, it is crucial that their output can be understood and justified by humans. The level of a model's interpretability - how easily its decisions are grasped by humans - has become a significant factor in making predictions and learning outcomes more reliable. In our study, we introduce a groundbreaking framework for measuring a model's interpretability by leveraging cognitive science principles and the psychological concept of cognitive complexity. This novel framework comprises three distinct layers of human learning and adaptation. The initial layer simulates human perception and encoding, the middle layer models human processing, and the final layer represents human recall and recognition. Each layer is equipped with an optimization algorithm designed to fine-tune the model's output, ensuring it accurately mirrors human cognition. We apply this framework to models trained on the IMDB dataset, determining the cognitive complexity of a model is directly linked to its accuracy in predicting sentiment. The framework is then used to assess the efficacy of distillation, revealing that a single layer of abstraction - specifically the storage layer - is capable of delivering a distiller that is substantially equivalent in performance to a traditional student, as measured against their respective teachers.

Anomaly detection without supervision is a critical issue in data analysis, particularly where identification of intrinsic characteristics in anomalies is impractical. Given the difficulties in acquiring labeled data, many algorithms have been developed to address this problem, with Isolation Forest being one such solution. This forest of isolated, isolated units efficiently identifies anomalies by isolating each data point quickly. However, its computational cost can be substantial for large datasets. We address these limitations in a novel version of Isolation Forest, adapted for use on embedded systems with limited resources. We enhance the algorithm by introducing a pre-filtering process, utilizing KNN for efficient detection, and exploring the potential benefits of weakly-guided anomaly detection. We evaluate the effectiveness of these methods through a range of experiments. We optimize the isolation process in IF by using KNN's nearest neighbors, reducing computational cost while maintaining accuracy. Additionally, incorporating a weakly-guided approach improves the accuracy of anomaly detection while retaining the isolation forest's simplicity. These discoveries enable the development of a isolation forest-based method with high potential, particularly in supervised learning scenarios.

A novel approach to calculating the probability distribution of extremely high events within a given time frame can be derived from a Bayesian analysis of a process where the occurrence of events follows a certain pattern of increase. By breaking this up into smaller, uniformly-distributed times and applying the distribution of these events according to their order, one can determine the frequency of extremely high events. This new method is related to a well-known technique called order statistics, which is used in situations where events follow a specific, uniformly-distributed pattern. Our approach, however, can be applied to scenarios where the frequency of events follows a Poisson distribution. This order statistics method, therefore, provides a useful tool for situations where the collection of events within a given time frame is limited. It is also more efficient, as it allows for the calculation of extremely high event frequencies within a given time frame through a simpler process, without requiring a more computationally demanding approach. This new order statistics method is then applied to a specific situation, where the frequency of extremely high events within a given year is to be calculated. It is compared with a couple of other models, including a simple equation and a more complicated, time-varying model. These comparisons show that the new approach is both accurate and reliable, providing results that are in line with the frequency of extremely high events within a given year. It is also adaptable, allowing for the calculation of extremely high event frequencies within a given month as well. This new approach is then applied to a specific

In nonlin/nonlin gauge theory, the average cross section remains constant across specific spatial areas, fixed for any given impact parameter, and does not depend on the target shape or properties. These regions are bounded by curves that rise in relation to impact parameters, and as impact cross sections increase, these regions expand in spatial terms. Notably, in cases where the target is a flat sheet, these regions coincide with areas where classical paths diverge.

To facilitate natural language understanding through machine learning, there is a growing need for structured knowledge that can be leveraged as a foundation. This study builds upon the ATOMIC knowledge base, which records causal relationships and effects in everyday language, to compare symbolic and neural foundations for natural language processing. The research team then demonstrates how the structured information within ATOMIC can be utilized to enhance tasks such as text classification and relation classification, achieving state-of-the-art results and exceeding the capabilities of non-foundational models. The study is made available online, including accompanying code at https://github.com/cometcog/comet-atomic-2020 and the dataset at https://github.com/cometcog/comet-atomic-2020-data. The research is accompanied by a detailed analysis of the dataset, as well as a comprehensive report, which can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.03073.

We present an overview of the data compression techniques employed by the Hi-GAL project, which leveraged high-quality data from the APEX and APEX-12m submillimeter telescopes to compress 112 source groups, representing the entire Hi-GAL spatial coverage, across five broad frequency bands. Our selected compression methods significantly reduced data size while preserving its comprehensive spectral and spatial content, ultimately resulting in freely accessible compressed data at CTA, VDA, and ALMA's helpdesk portals. Furthermore, we detail specific data compression strategies applied to the GLADE catalogue which encompasses information on 77,114 individual sources, their respective counterparts in the IRAS, MSX, and WISE spectral range, and their respective IRAS data at 60 μm, 100 μm, and 240 μm, with an added warning on IRAS' higher frequency bands due to limited data availability.

The study of metal-poor, ancient stars within globular clusters offers valuable insights into early cosmic enrichment. However, the presence of these extremely metal-poor stars cannot be readily detected by conventional spectroscopy due to their weak emission lines. This limitation has largely been resolved with the FLAMES-UVES spectrograph on the Very Large Telescope (VLT), which has enabled researchers to study such faint stars precisely. Our analysis focuses on five extremely metal-poor (~Baan-Goss) stars in the rich globular cluster NGC~2808, utilizing high-resolution spectroscopy with UVES. Our results reveal that these stars have comparable iron abundance but distinct magnesium levels, confirming a spread in metal content among these stars. The iron-hydrogen ratio and helium abundance of the calculated isochrones for NGC~2808 match corresponding models. The data suggest that enriched hydrogen and helium were present in the cluster during the initial phase of star formation in NGC~2808, likely due to either capturing primordial gas or returning enriched material through various processes. The candidate horizontal branch stars with varying magnesium levels offer essential clues on the initial metal distribution within the cluster. The presence of magnesium lines in candidate second generation stars presents an opportunity to investigate the initial spatial distribution within the cluster. The data for these stars have been added to the study. Our analysis of the cluster suggests it contains no primordial stars with temperatures above 7000K, indicating a possible turn-off from the lower generation stars with higher metal content.

We develop and validate a numerical method for single file diffusion to analyze the duration of first exit times for an overdamped Brownian particle within a one-dimensional track with entropic barriers. The first exit time analysis is applied to both escape scenarios from localized wells and disordered energy landscapes. By examining first exit time distributions, we determine the speed of localization and the frequency distribution of the localization point near the barrier, as well as the speed of approach and the frequency distribution of the particle's speed when it crosses the barrier. These characteristics provide insights into the physical processes of localizing and escaping from a localized state, especially in the presence of disorder. The validity of our results is supported by comparing them to existing literature on escape problems from localized wells.

Although quantum mechanics accurately predicts a wide range of phenomena, it lacks a comprehensive theoretical framework for making reliable measurements.  To address this gap, a new quantum version of Bayes' rule has been developed to facilitate the interpretation of quantum measurement results.  This quantum rule has been effectively applied to a significant study on the interference of low-temperature GaAs nanoring electrons.  In this study, multiple nanorings have been arranged to facilitate coherent interference among electrons emitted from different rings, enabling the visualization of quantum paths through a quantum version of an interpretative formula.  By utilizing the quantum Bayes' rule, researchers have been able to accurately interpret experimental results and validate the consistency of quantum mechanics.  This approach has been found to be versatile and can be applied to the analysis of quantum phenomena in various fields, including optics and cold-atom research.

The normalization factor used for scaling $P_{long}$ and $D^{~N}$ off to infinite momentum is denoted by $Q_{0}$. This factor is determined by minimizing $\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{\sigma_{ Long}}{\sigma_{T}}-1\right)^{2}$, where $\frac{\sigma_{Long}}{\sigma_{T}}$ is the long- and transverse cross sectional ratio. This normalization factor is then applied to $D^{~N}$ and $J/\psi$ to find $Q_{0}$ as functions of $p_{T}$ and $N_{part}$. These relationships are then used to calculate the $B_{N}$ of $D^{~N}$ and $J/\psi$ in terms of $N_{part}$ and $p_{T}$. The $B_{N}$ of $D^{~N}$ is found to be less than that of $J/\psi$ by a factor that increases with $p_{T}$ and $N_{part}$. The $B_{N}$ of $D^{~N}$ and $J/\psi$ is found to decrease as $p_{T}$ increases for the same $N_{part}$. The top-dimensional cohomology group in the mod 2 cohomology space of the Steenrod algebra, denoted by R-alg, contains a subgroup generated by squ( R) when R is a non-trivial 2-torsion-containing ring R, where the operation is pointwise multiplication. 

Further consideration shows the above generation result holds for the entire graded cohomology group in the case of a one-dimensional ring R. However, for a three-dimensional ring R that contains two-dimensional ring R contains no 2-torsion, the Steenrod algebra's cohomology group's generation by squ( R) fails.

Astronomers studying the ultraviolet region face significant challenges due to the high intensity of Lyman-alpha emission from the Earth's atmosphere, which necessitates the use of radiation filters. However, researchers working at ultraviolet wavelengths with higher sensitivities than space-based telescopes require different filters. Developed by the Lyman Space-blind Filter prototype, this is a ground-based technology that eliminates Earth's Lyman-alpha emission, enabling accurate ultraviolet spectral measurements. This innovative filter uses a microstructured hologram within a silicon carbide cell and exhibits excellent performance by minimizing Lyman-alpha emission to -0.1% and maintaining transmission above 90%. The advantages of this technology could also be applied to developing a cryogenic filter for use in laboratory and experimental physics procedures.

This study addresses the challenge of managing complex graph-based systems in an optimal manner through the effective communication among their nodes. Graph filters, comprising a convolutional operation and a convolutional filter, are utilized to achieve a desired output or behavior within these systems, akin to control. By leveraging Fourier analysis and its limitations due to irregularities, as well as the additional constraints of inverting the graph, which can lead to exponentially high computational costs, conventional approaches are often prohibitively expensive or impractical. In contrast, this work presents a novel, decentralized method capable of directly estimating the optimal graph filter within each node using a message-passing scheme, eliminating the need for global processing and resulting in a scalable, efficient solution.

Image search algorithms on large databases are limited by their capacity for processing images at high speeds, despite recent advancements in hardware that enable more efficient methods like hashing and pivots. One major limitation is the indexing dynamic dataset problem, which remains unresolved. Current image indexing techniques vary depending on the specific algorithm being used, such as $k$-means for random forests, but these techniques fail to adapt to dynamic datasets. In this paper, we present a novel indexing technique that uses hierarchical clustering to facilitate efficient indexing of dynamic datasets in hardware, resulting in significant speed improvements for retrieval operations. We introduce an efficient clustering algorithm based on block-wise mean normalization that reduces computation, incorporates our indexing technique, and maintains real-time search performance. We test our indexing technique across multiple hardware environments and evaluate its effectiveness across various hardware architectures.

This study verifies the feasibility of a novel, unsupervised approach to error correction for binary linear codes within Gaussian noise. The developed algorithm, drawing on ideas from combinatorial optics and differential geometry, does not require initial transmission of encoded data, instead using received signals as its starting point to create a map between noisy space and a transformed version of noisy space, where each point corresponds to a code word with maximum likely accuracy. Notably, this unsupervised method exhibits performance comparable to the best possible performance for binary linear codes of limited size, slightly exceeding it for larger code sizes. When used for decoding binary linear codes of various sizes within Gaussian noise, this unsupervised method demonstrates results comparable to the best possible performance for low error rates and slightly exceeded it for higher error rates.

The evolution of a particle in a specific type of nonlinear potential, known as a washed-out potential, exhibits unique characteristics in the phase space. Despite the presence of friction, the particle's speed remains constant over time. This article will provide an in-depth explanation of this phenomenon, along with evidence that a wide range of potentials, including those with nonlinear characteristics, share this behavior. Our analysis will offer a mathematical proof of this effect, making this phenomenon applicable to a much broader range of physical systems.

This research aims to develop a dynamic perspective on the economic impacts of unexpected shocks, such as those resulting from monetary policy changes, natural disasters, and financial crises. By employing a probabilistic approach to time series modeling through Random Forest theory, we can establish causal links and determine reaction patterns to sudden events. Utilizing data from 34 countries under the Inflation Targeting framework, our analysis indicates that the effects of sudden shocks vary in nature and intensity over time. Notably, our findings reveal both short-term and long-term responses, as evidenced by significant changes in interest rates and stock prices, with effects becoming more pronounced approximately 20 months after the initial shock. Moreover, our research shows that the response to such shocks is not uniform and is instead influenced by specific factors, including country risk levels, with higher-risk countries exhibiting more pronounced long-term reactions to sudden events.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on a charge rotating in a magnetic field, which results in significant angular momentum transfer, or the 'Casimir effect on angular momentum transfer,' between the charge and the surrounding vacuum. Specifically, our research derived an expression for this effect that is based on the charge's angular velocity, the magnetic field strength, and the distance between the charge and the boundaries. Furthermore, it has been discovered that the'stirring' effect that occurs when the charge is placed near a boundary is not only limited to that boundary but is actually a general phenomenon that occurs when the charge is placed near any closed curve, which would lead to the extraction of angular momentum from the vacuum and transfer it to the charge. This effect is actually a case of a third-order phase transition that occurs when the charge is placed near a boundary. This research also opened the door for studying similar effects in which the quantum vacuum induces changes in the mechanical properties of mirrors, which was a topic of discussion in the paper's conclusion section.

As the complexity of text grows, precision in naming entity is crucial for extracting valuable information, but current methods struggle with accuracy due to the linear scale of text and entity embeddings. To address this challenge, we develop FGNET-RH, a sophisticated named entity classification model that utilizes a semi-supervised refinement process within hyperbolic space, combining the advantages of hierarchical and flat models. Our approach yields impressive results, with the entity classes hierarchy extracted automatically, and significant accuracy improvements, with up to an 8.79% boost on the benchmark dataset.

This paper establishes upper limits on the Hankel determinants $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(4)(f)$ for functions within the univalent class $\mathcal{U}$ and the general unstarred class $\mathcal{S}$ by utilizing the well-known monotone representation of Fejér-Riesz. Specifically, it shows that $H_2(3)(f) \le 8$ and $H_2(4)(f) \le 32$, with equalities achieved for $f(z) = z$. For the starlike class $\mathcal{U}_*$, we obtain $H_2(3)(f) \le 4$, with an equality reached for $f(z) = z e^{i \theta}$ and the maximum value of $\theta$ occurring at $\theta = 2.7639$. Similarly, for the starlike univalent class $\mathcal{U}_{*} \mathcal{S}$, we obtain $H_2(4)(f) \le 16$, with an equality reached for $f(z) = z e^{i \theta} \operatorname{csz} (a z)$ and the maximum value of $\theta$ and $a$ occurring at $\theta = 2.7639$ and $a = 0.7479$.

To achieve reliable QoS in cloud computing data centers, each virtual machine is allocated guaranteed computing resources, but this leads to poor performance when the sum of reserved resources exceeds the actual available capacity. Therefore, managing reserved resources efficiently is crucial for providing quality services. This study presents Prepartition - a static reservation reallocation method for improving computing resource utilization in data centers by minimizing waste resulting from prior resource reservations, especially in scenarios with dynamically changing workloads. Prepartition achieves this through two main techniques: nested virtualization and ejection, which reorder reservation requests and adjust computing resources accordingly, all while ensuring the satisfaction of existing requests. This approach dynamically updates the reallocation policy based on the current workload, thereby achieving optimal performance. Our results indicate that Prepartition achieves significant gains in terms of average response time and energy efficiency compared to the Flat model and Progressive model. For example, in cases with beta-distributed workload fluctuations, Prepartition yields 14.5% and 60.4% improvements in response time and energy efficiency respectively, whereas in scenarios with exponentially distributed fluctuations, Prepartition achieves 1.7% and 22.8% improvements in response time and energy efficiency respectively.

We're focusing on the most basic type of game, where two agents make decisions based on the predictions of how the other will act. This type of game has two equilibrium points: one where neither forecasts the other to change and one where they forecast each other to change. We're investigating the feasibility of using machine learning models that can learn and predict these equilibrium points. We found that certain types of machine learning models that utilize neural networks can accurately predict these equilibrium points, but others may not be as effective. We also discovered that some models that can't learn may get stuck in suboptimal predictions. We're exploring ways to modify these models so they can accurately predict both equilibrium points.

In data analysis, understanding the causal influence provides valuable insights into model probability and result interpretation. Causal influences measure how much each potential parent impacts the subsequent causal effects between other model variables and the response, as opposed to the overall influence, which can be much wider in scope. We derive tight bounds between these measures, expressing the causal influence as a fraction of the overall influence. For Gaussian models, we establish that the causal influence is at most $O((\log p)^{d+1})$ when the model dimension is $p$ and the number of variables is $d$. In systems with Gaussian or Bernoulli distributions, we improve upon a key finding in (Kalnins et al. 2020) regarding the upper bound of their Algorithm 1 by eliminating the $O(\log\log p)$ term.

This research aims to enhance operational safety by enabling early detection of anomalies in real-time, due to unforeseen events or covert attacks, which can be triggered by sudden changes in measured system data. Since sudden changes may indicate anomalies, our proposal introduces a straightforward yet reliable test that uses difference dynamics to identify anomalies in systems affected by attacks. We have demonstrated that our test can identify anomalies in line with Bayesian estimation methods, and offer a efficient statistical interpretation of the test's results, which can be applied to any linear time-invariant system. Furthermore, our test can be applied to any predictive model used for measurement correction in systems, such as Kalman filter-based models, to effectively monitor system health in real-time. We have verified the effectiveness of our test in identifying anomalies caused by attacks for a target system modeled after a 2019 drone published in the Journal of Aerospace Engineering (JAE).

A precise summary provides users with a concise overview of complex documents, making it a vital tool in both personal and professional life. Current English language models have achieved significant success, but those designed for Indian languages continue to struggle due to a lack of advanced techniques and available datasets. Our research presents a new method, GAE-ISumm, to create summaries automatically for news articles in five Indian languages using a graph-based approach, leveraging external knowledge sources to enhance quality. By applying our technique to 1,825 news articles across these languages, we demonstrate its effectiveness using standard evaluation metrics. Additionally, our analysis highlights the significance of syntactic similarities and knowledge-based phrases in producing accurate summaries. Compared to existing external knowledge source models, our results demonstrate that our method produces summaries with higher coherence and relevance. The performance of GAE-ISumm surpasses existing models, achieving a high F1 score of 0.054, marking it as the first successful application of graph-based summery for Indian languages.

We explore right perfect Cohen rings over a Prüfer p-ring with the form R = <T1,...,TN>, having a p-adic transcendence degree. Our research extends the lifting and lifting base characteristics of S-rings to characteristic p for every positive integer p. Moreover, our results precisely define the lifting base characteristic of R in relation to each subring of R. We establish the existence of a p-partition of R for every p in a subset of the set of prime numbers, which makes R an S-ring with p-partition for all p in a subset of the set of prime numbers. Our results strictly extend the lifting base characteristic of S-rings from characteristic p to characteristic p for every positive integer p.
