Furthermore, numerical evaluations illustrate that the RIS-aided OFDM system can achieve notable gains in terms of BER performance, specifically up to 3dB at a BER of

The integral variation theorem established by Aharony et al. in 2001 has significant implications for understanding quantum entanglement, particularly in terms of its relationship between entropy and correlations. By leveraging single-energy entropy measurements, the theorem concludes that any non-projective quantum density operator displayed on its von Neumann entropy also manifests correlations. This study reveals that in the absence of projective measurements, a density operator's non-zero entropy does not necessarily imply non-zero entropy in its reduced operators. Notably, our analysis encompasses cases where the density operator has non-zero entropy, as well as cases where local operators have zero entropy. To investigate this phenomenon, we have selectively chosen various density operators, demonstrating that while some exhibit non-zero entropy throughout their reductions, others feature multiple reductions with zero entropy coexisting with a density operator having non-zero entropy.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons within a nearly G2 geometry.  When applying this theory to Euclidean G2-instantons, our results reveal that deformations map directly to 3-form self-dual cohomology classes, explaining an earlier finding by Chae.  An associated infinitesimal deformation theorem is also derived and proves that minimal G2-instantons have no deformations, aligning with the findings of Bogdanoval, Chae, and Sasaki for four-dimensional self-dual conformal geometry.

The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused widespread losses,
 resulting in countless lives lost. As the virus continues to evolve, countries
 have implemented a range of measures to slow its spread. Among these measures,
 contact tracing programs, which aim to track the infection source while adhering
 to strict data protection protocols, have become increasingly common. The
 success of contact tracing relies heavily on user engagement. A core component
 of contact tracing apps is their ability to record location data, which raises
 substantial concerns regarding user privacy. This paper analyzes the privacy
 features of contact tracing apps from seven countries, examining their compliance
 with established data protection standards. Our investigation focuses on the
 following countries: Germany, the UK, Singapore, Italy, China, Netherlands, and
 Spain, with our research revealing significant inconsistencies in data security
 across the studied countries. Specifically, we evaluate the location, access,
 and storage security of contact tracing app data, identifying specific vulnerabilities
 in the process. Our analysis emphasizes the importance of robust technical
 measures in maintaining public and user privacy.

Recent findings indicate that the human brain undergoes changes at the quantum level
when engaged in complex tasks such as learning and memory. Researchers now aim to
harvest and utilize quantum data from the brain, which presents an initial challenge.
Firstly, we'll examine the current understanding of quantum information theory and its
relevance to neuroscience. Next, we'll discuss existing experiments that have shown
quantum processing in the human brain, focusing on patterns discovered in experiments
involving quantum data from stimulation experiments. Furthermore, we'll explore the
importance of distinguishing between thermal noise and true quantum information in neural
research. After that, we'll delve into the feasibility of extracting and utilizing quantum
data from the brain, including the potential applications and difficulties in harvesting
quantum data. Finally, we'll outline possible future pathways for leveraging quantum
data in the human brain and related technological implications, which may also raise some
ethical considerations.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into native C code and verifying its correctness through the development of an ACL2 theorem library. By embedding a restricted version of C within a subset of ACL2, we can translate ACL2 functions representing C expressions into their equivalent C forms, which can then be generated directly. The tool aims to utilize existing ACL2 proof tools to provide C code verification without requiring off-site access to these tools. Although our current implementation has limitations, specifically with functions possessing side effects and utilizing diverse data types, it serves as a potential foundation for developing more comprehensive solutions in the future.

A notable YORO family, comprising 101 members, has drawn significant attention with its YUV three-body weak resonances. Notably, researchers have highlighted a novel three-body weak resonance by analyzing PVS, suggesting the YUV configuration might be optimal for a four-body strong resonance, further justifying the YORO designation. By employing SWROs, the YUV three-body weak resonance has been fully explained, providing a deeper understanding of this phenomenon. By exploring the TQ family as a comparator, scientists have discovered that the YUV four-body strong resonance has a significantly later arrival time than its counterpart in the SWRO configuration, further designating the YORO family as an exceptional case.

Ramanujan proposed a conjecture regarding the exact formulas for particular solutions to the Hurwitz zeta function, specifically $\zeta(s, a)$ for an odd $a$ and specific values of $s$. This article presents intermediate results derived from evaluating the quadratic factor of the associated theta type zeta function, as well as evidence suggesting a strong connection between this function and solutions to the equation $s=1/2 + 2\pi i\alpha$, which correlates with periodic elements of the upper half-plane. These results are also linked to the properties of complex Eisenstein series.

We demonstrate in this note that the elliptic cohomology theory $E$, as developed by Porter--Tabuada for spaces like CP(V), shares essential characteristics with the  elliptic cohomology theory $\ell$ first described by Lawrence--Quinn for spaces like CP(V). Notably, our  computation of the ring of cohomology for CP(V) in both $E$ and $\ell$ reveals it to be isomorphic to the ring of  cohomology for V, specifically showing that E(V) isomorphic to $\ell(V)$. Given an action by a finite group G on V, we  further ensure that both E and $\ell$ are equivariantly preserved under this action. As a result, the theories  $E^{G}$ and $\ell^{G}$ are identifiable, and their ring of cohomology in both $E^{G}$ and $\ell^{G}$ in  relation to V is preserved under the action of G.

We employ algebraic topology, the study of persistent homologies through different scales of filter applications, to analyze complex physical systems. By leveraging a charting method that utilizes machine learning for generating scales of filter sizes, we enhance the topological analysis. The proposed framework combines a machine learning approach with the Fredholm determinant to visualize and understand the persistent homologies' evolution over different scales. An unsupervised learning method is then developed for obtaining the algebraic structures of the filtered spaces, represented as graphs. The proposed graph-based architecture captures the topological properties of the filtered spaces. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to two systems: (i) a perturbed torus and (ii) a rotating deformed neutron.

This paper provides a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order examination of the angular distributions in $J/\psi$ production through $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c, \chi_{cJ}$ ($J=0,1,2$) using the nonrelativistic QCD factorization method (NRQCD). The study derives the numerical outcomes of the NRQCD angular distributions at the energy level of $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV and evaluates the best-fit results for the dominant nonrelativistic charmonium content in the $J/\psi$ system. The analysis further includes a numerical assessment of the dominant binding energies $\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{D} \to \eta_c} \approx 340 \mathrm{MeV}$ and $\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{D} \to \chi_{cJ}} \approx 620 \mathrm{MeV}$ in the dijet systems $\mathrm{D} \to J/\psi \eta_c$ and $\mathrm{D} \to J/\psi \chi_{cJ}$ respectively.

Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who understand the function of PINs (enthusiasts) and those who do not (casual users). Surprisingly, only 14% of users declined to use a PIN, indicating successful encouragement of Signal's features. While enthusiastic users predominantly employed complex PINs, casual users mainly used simple ones. Interestingly, casual users who shared their PINs with more people primarily did so out of a sense of obligation. These findings suggest that educating casual users and addressing unnecessary features' complexity are prime focuses for improvement initiatives.

This study presents a method for accurately calculating the solar flux through a product of functions, given the user, by employing Gaussian quadrature techniques. We investigate the properties of the resulting quadrature rule, with a focus on creating a method that is both efficient and implements easily. Our proposed scheme consists of a combination of rules with varying point counts: 1, 2, 3, 5, and 7 points. We not only determine the corresponding coordinates and weights but also analyze the associated error terms, making the rule implementable in procedures using floating point arithmetic. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the quadrature rule's adaptability to various applications, such as the computation of solar flux through a blackbody function and the numerical solution of radiative transfer equations. We compare the proposed quadrature rule with the existing approaches in the field, and through the examples presented, we demonstrate the advantage of the new method in terms of both efficiency and accuracy.

The second derivative, or curvature, of a function, specifically its Hessian matrix, holds significant value in understanding function behavior, particularly in machine learning where it's used to optimize training. However, capturing this derivative accurately is rare due to computational limitations and previous practical limitations. Many studies have modeled or approximated this derivative but none as efficiently as this study suggests, utilizing the generalized Gauss-Newton's low-rank framework. 

This study provides an efficient algorithm to accurately capture the derivative, or Hessian, with theoretical justification for its efficiency and effectiveness. It also demonstrates the efficacy of this approach through comprehensive analysis and real-world applications, opening doors for future applications. 

The key to this study's achievement of computational efficiency lies in leveraging the generalized Gauss-Newton's low-rank framework to capitalize on the low-rank nature of gradient matrices in non-convex problems and viViT's ability to maintain closed-form property, or Hessian matrix, in many scenarios. 

Theoretical justification for this approach is provided through mathematical proof of its accuracy and computational efficiency. 

The study also tackles potential viViT limitations by proving its effectiveness in various parameter settings. 

It's worth noting that this study's proposals for computational efficiency are specific to curved geometry, or Hessian matrix, which is uncommon in literature. 

The study's findings are further validated through comprehensive analysis and real-world applications, or Hessian matrix, which are crucial in understanding function behavior, particularly in machine learning where it's used to

In languages that distinguish nouns by grammatical gender, a limited class of words changes their class when combined with articles or adjectives. To examine how this "grammatical gender" class affects how we think about words, we created a dataset of 2000 German nouns from a training-based brain-computer interface and looked at how people with this technology rank related words. Our analysis shows that people tended to group nouns by grammatical gender, even when we removed clues like articles and made it hard to figure out this class from the words themselves. When we compared this to how people think about nouns in languages without grammatical gender, we found that we tend to group related words by the same categories, but not by this "grammatical gender" class. Based on this, we think that grammatical gender might be a clue that our brains use to make connections between related words, but this effect seems to be pretty specific to how we combine words with articles and adjectives in our language.

The charmability of a finite group is the maximum size of its smallest non-trivial normal subgroup. We determine the charmability of simple algebraic groups over non Archimedean local fields with positive charactristic, categorifying the results from char 0. We also investigate the charmability of split Chevalley groups and all classical groups in positive char, using this framework. Furthermore, the concept of stiffness is introduced, corresponding to the rigidity of groups under inner automorphisms, and its relationship with charmability is established.

Traditional methods for estimating object positions rely on classical color and depth data. However, color-based approaches suffer from classification inaccuracies, while depth-based methods struggle with occlusion issues. To address these limitations, a new object positioning method utilizes category-level data, effectively handling multi-person scenarios in complex environments. This innovative approach involves two main components: a real-time, color-based object detector and a depth-based localization system, which together provide accurate object position estimates. The proposed method is successfully tested on challenging video datasets such as the Posetrack multi-person dataset and the Street-to-Room dataset, which simulates indoor scenarios. The experimental results demonstrate the method's superiority over existing object positioning techniques. Additionally, a novel evaluation metric is introduced to measure performance in real-world scenarios. The proposed method's source code is made available for public use.

The complex nature of traffic forecasting, particularly regarding the sparsity problem, has hindered the development of effective prediction methods. In this challenge, the main task is to leverage historical and real-time road usage to generate future traffic volume, despite sparse data. To address this issue, we first introduce a novel framework that utilizes similarity analysis to fill in missing data across time and space, and then refine time-series data for forecast generation. Our approach, dubbed Similarity-based Attribute Extraction for Sparse Traffic Forecasting (SAE-STF), consists of three key components: Similarity Calculation, Feature Extraction, and Neural Forecasting. To validate our approach, we implemented it within the Microsoft Azure AutoML platform and competed in the 2022 Traffic4cast Challenge, where we achieved outstanding results, ranking 1st, 2nd, and 3rd in the "Lampost'22: Open Data" track for 1-hour, 2-hour, and 4-hour forecasting windows, respectively. Moreover, our team achieved impressive results in the 2021 Traffic4cast Challenge, ranking 1st in the 'No Open Data' track for 1-hour forecasting (mean absolute percentage error: 0.01%), and 2nd for 2-hour and 4-hour forecasting (mean absolute percentage error: 0.16% and 0.31%).

This study presents VACA, a model that generates predictive models through variational graph autoencoders to handle complex, real-world datasets in policy evaluation and counterfactual analysis. By using existing datasets within established platforms, such as OpenLIFT and ProPublica's LIFT, VACA facilitates the exploration of causal influences under real-world conditions. Unlike earlier approaches relying on surrogate models, VACA generates predictive models directly from data. As a result, it excels at handling large-scale, intensive counterfactual analysis tasks. VACA's versatility is demonstrated through its application to both pseudo-experimental settings and actual intervention-based experiments. Moreover, it effectively considers crucial factors like global history, previous treatment decisions, and temporal treatment sequences in counterfactual analysis. When applied to ProPublica's LIFT dataset, VACA accurately predicts outcomes based on actual intervention outcomes. By using causal representation learning, VACA's results in pseudo-experimental and intervention-based environments exhibit practical applicability and theoretical relevance.

The full potential of LOFAR's real-time capabilities hasn't been extensively explored, despite being fully operational since 2018. Our research presents data from the REALTA system, which enabled the collection and quick processing (every ten seconds) of all LOFAR data flowing through the Irish station. We found REALTA to be highly sensitive, with its system delivering detection capabilities beyond that of dedicated surveys like GLEAM. The high output results from combining individual REALTA data streams suggest that this technology has vast applications in scientific research, including the analysis of single beams, the 48 LOFAR telescope configuration known as the European Low Frequency Array (LEA), and the 50 antenna "Superterp" at the Irish station. Our discoveries also indicate the high efficiency REALTA brings to the execution of scientific research initiatives, such as the search for Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) and the identification of rotating vector model sources. Our research sets a significant standard for future LOFAR extensions known as "Stations 2.0," which will be operational in 2022.

Machine learning-based modeling has become an indispensable tool in optimal design of metamaterials for specific functions. However, the application of machine learning in photonic systems remains relatively underexplored. We demonstrate a novel approach to designing metasurfaces that control photon flow through scattering and can be used to create complex light-hitting surfaces. Utilizing a machine learning-based reverse design method, our team successfully developed an efficient metasurface that enables near-perfect, omnidirectional visibility of coherent light waves traveling through normal incidence, even in systems with limited confinement of light energy. This advancement paves the way for practical applications of metasurfaces in photonic systems.

This study addresses the challenge of predicting box office revenue for upcoming movies.
Our unique dataset of 1574 movies comprises novel character diversity metrics and a range of demographic attributes.
To demonstrate the value of each factor, we analyzed correlation coefficients, discovered that star power has a significant impact on revenue, and developed an enhanced model integrating all these attributes, which outperformed previous proposals by achieving an R-squared value of 0.210.

The Alternative Frequency Control (AFC) method has effectively maintained electricity frequency stability across decades, but its latest evolution aims to enhance system stability, particularly addressing voltage fluctuations. Building on traditional AFC designs, this updated approach separates voltage and real power control, prioritizing frequency stability while maintaining steady voltage levels. This revised design encompasses multiple AC power sources and uses the derivative of voltage instead of voltage in the control signal, reducing the inherent voltage dynamics in the system. Consequently, this solution ensures consistent frequency stability and precise power output. To validate its performance, the proposed AFC was tested in a simulation based on a nonlinear model of a power system featuring multiple generators. Compared to traditional AFC designs, the new control method exhibits reduced voltage dynamics and improved stability, demonstrating its capabilities in repelling equilibrium points and providing overall system stability.

The integration of physical and cyber components within distributed systems leads to the development of cyberphysical systems, merging two distinct worlds into one. Analyzing such systems often requires unique, hybrid approaches that combine tools from autonomous linear quadratic expert system theory and cyberphysical system modeling. Existing research primarily focuses on the latter, neglecting the potential benefits of a more unified view. This dissertation aims to fill this knowledge gap by exploring the implications of the proposed theory. Furthermore, it demonstrates that foundational results in the proposed field can be derived from established methods, including matrix inequalities and maximum entropy techniques. Ultimately, it outlines potential avenues for future research within this new field of study.

Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions exhibit an increased Scattered Emission Component (SEC) in the UV and X-ray bands. However, understanding this component remains a challenge due to the complexities of treating polarized high-energy photons interacting through the Inverse Compton process via electrons, especially when these electrons are simulated using Monte-Carlo methods within the relativistic electrons' equipartition limit. To address this, a modified Monte-Carlo code for Inverse Compton scattering has been developed, taking into consideration the polarization of photons, even at MeV levels, and this code has been applied to the blazar object 3C 4543, observing a significant decrease in the UV excess, but an increased X-ray excess if the UV excess is real.

We focus on a function defined by its Taylor series with coefficients determined by integrals of a given function over infinitesimally small intervals in $\mathbb{R}$. By considering these coefficients as variables that take on irrational values, we study the properties of the resulting power series. Our investigation shows that the differentiability class of the power series is preserved under certain changes in its parameters, which aligns with Weyl's unitary equidistribution principle. Furthermore, this finding can be applied to an integral that appears in the study of traveling wave railgun dynamics by Arnold and Tresch, revealing its differentiability class. For a landscape $E$ defined by an even function $E(s)=-\frac{1}{\sin^2 s}$, we demonstrate that the corresponding power series analytically extends to a multivalued function, which can be represented as an elliptic function. This extension facilitates the characterization of the differentiability class of the original function $E$ and its higher-order derivatives up to a certain derivative order. For another landscape $E(z)=-z^4+z$, we demonstrate that the corresponding power series analytically extends to a multivalued function, which can be represented as a composition of elementary functions, which satisfies specific conditions.

Notably, identifying pure state symmetries in quantum states without projective measurements is challenging, especially since performing projective measurements destroys the very symmetry one wishes to identify. To overcome this limitation, we investigate the use of adaptive measurement strategies, which redefine what constitutes an optimal measurement for exposing state symmetries. We demonstrate that within a fixed budget of queries, there are optimal adaptive measurement sequences that successfully detect any given symmetric pure state. We have successfully applied our method to accurately classify Bell-like states, previously thought to be indeistinguishable through minimal measurements, despite possessing distinct symmetries.

Baryon formation is explored through the fragmentation of a QCD string quantized in space and time. A novel helical structure is adopted for the QCD string, characterized by quantized and interlinked baryon constituent constituents. Three color flux tubes emerge from a quantized and twisted QCD string, carrying charges corresponding to baryon quark components. Quantized fragmentons and additional quark and anti-quark components arise from the QCD string fragmentation, with lattice Reggeon Field Theory calculations indicating that baryon formation demands at least three quark components. Three quark configurations host baryon charges, while excess quark components form mesons.

The study conducted an in-depth examination of how solar activity areas impact helioseismic travel time measurements through a global model representing global surface velocity patterns. It was discovered that by shifting the model's reference point from the Sun's equator to a south-facing pole, the amplitude of helioseismic wave phase speed changed by approximately -83 cm/s. The study revealed that to cause this alteration through a radial displacement, solar activity areas must experience a net movement of about 10 m/s in a southward direction. It was observed that to achieve this, solar activity areas' overall rotation speed needs to be roughly 20 km/s higher than the surrounding areas. The study found that to explain the helioseismic travel time measurements, solar activity areas' increased rotation speed should be confined to approximately 20% of the total circumference in each direction. The study showed that to achieve the required net movement, solar activity areas' rotation speed should be higher by about 5-25 m/s compared to the surrounding areas. The study concluded that to explain helioseismic travel time measurements, solar activity areas' rotation speed should be higher by about 20 m/s.

Researchers from the NANOGrav, Parkes, European, and International Pulsar Timing Array collaborations have detected potential fluctuations in the pace of neutron star rotation, which may be caused by waves generated at an early stage of the universe. Specifically, their analysis suggests that a specific type of gravitational disturbance in the 10^-18 Hz frequency range, which could be a sign of long-standing magnetic field tensions, is consistent with recently observed trends in the Pulsar Timing Array data. Although no conclusive evidence has been found, further research indicates the possibility of detecting a similar disturbance in the upcoming future.

Light field technology is currently a focus of interest for the development of innovative applications in the fields of photography and rendering. However, its high dimensionality, with a storage requirement proportional to the square of the viewing angles, hinders its practical use in industry. To overcome this limitation, techniques such as compression and reconstruction are employed, with existing approaches focusing on simplifying the light field's representation. This research focuses on developing novel methods for compressing and reconstructing light fields, specifically by discretizing the scene into non-overlapping regions. A key contribution of this work involves proposing a novel learning-based approach for compressing light fields by employing a position-based model of axial parity, which treats pixel positions as markers that follow certain rules during reconstruction. This is achieved through the employment of a specialized neural network, specifically a Transformer model, that utilizes pixel positions to generate high-quality and clear images in all views, utilizing a shared encoder for shared features. Additionally, a positional attention mechanism is introduced, which analyzes the spatial relationships between pixels in each view, thus contributing to the creation of a more detailed and clear scene. This is achieved through the employment of two separate transformers, which analyze the spatial relationships between pixels in each view, thus contributing to the creation of a a more detailed and clear light field. Lastly, a positional attention mechanism is proposed, which analyzes the spatial relationships between pixels in each view, thus enabling a more accurate and clear light field to be created.

This paper presents a novel approach to enhance vector-based cross-lingual search by leveraging the strengths of both interactive and non-interactive models. To achieve this, we incorporate a multi-stage retrieval process that integrates query embeddings from both types of models, with a soft consensus mechanism to determine the final ranking. Notably, our method can be applied without modifying the existing models or fine-tuning them, making it highly efficient. Experimental results on a multilingual web corpus demonstrate that this combined approach significantly improves performance, with query-to-query average precision rates of 7.44% and 12.16% for English-French and English-Chinese cross-lingual search, respectively, when compared to using a single non-interactive model.

The importance of accurate health data at the global, national, and local levels has led to an increased focus on survey design and data modeling in developing countries. In this research, we compared the effectiveness of different health data modeling approaches, including both spatial and temporal models, with a focus on low and middle income countries. Our analysis revealed that the combination of baseline data and subsequent short series modeling, using either spatial or temporal methods, is the most reliable approach, but only when accounting for spatial patterns provides results comparable to imputation techniques. Our findings also suggest that the success of these methods depends heavily on the quality of the baseline data, emphasizing the need for more efforts in designing comprehensive health surveys. Our research offers insights and recommendations for future health data modeling efforts in low and middle income countries.

We develop a modern betting technique inspired by Kelly's statistical principle, incorporating quantum mechanics into the betting process. By utilizing a two-mode squeezed vacuum state as a bank's capital, as well as two-phase rotation induced by beam splitters, we generate a variable betting fund. Distinguishing itself from traditional Kelly methods, this approach utilizes continuous variable techniques to create the betting fund, thereby allowing exploration of quantum states as betting options in addition to the use of traditional funds. As a result, the novel funding method possesses inherent multifunctionality. Moreover, within the context of continuous variable betting, a quantum betting strategy emerges that treats the bank's capital as a two-mode squeezed vacuum state, thereby treating the betting fund and gambling stakes as interchangeable entities. In doing so, a new betting technique is demonstrated that treats the bank's capital as a combination of quantum states, thereby facilitating the adoption of the quantum Bayesian approach. As such, the novel funding method possesses inherent multifunctionality. Furthermore, the methods employed to create the betting fund and the generation of two-mode squeezed vacuum states can be viewed as interdependent and mutually applicable techniques, thereby allowing the adoption of the quantum Bayesian approach. As a consequence, a new betting technique emerges that treats the bank's capital as a combination of quantum states, thereby facilitating the adoption of the quantum Bayesian approach. As such, the novel funding method possesses inherent multifunctionality.

The recently created compound MA$_2$Z$_4$ (M = Mo, W, Ti; A= Si, Ge; Z = N, P, As), exhibiting an orthorhombic Polymorphism MoSi$_2$Z$_4$ structure with both horizontal stacking single layers and vertical interaction, is claimed to show potential in generating single-layer superconductors, thanks to the existence of an energetically favorable two-layer supercell. Through the use of calculated band structures, the influence of different horizontal stacking structures on the band arrangement of quasiparticle is identified, however, the horizontal band structure structure is independent of the stacking structure, which results in the existence of a unique exciton across different horizontal stacking structures. Furthermore, the horizontal band structure structure is suggested to influence the horizontal stacking structure, which results in the existence of unique excitons in the MoSi$_2$Z$_4$ and GeSi$_2$Z$_4$ compounds that could lead to potential superconductivity at specific pressure levels.

The decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ has been examined for mutual momentum and the muon charge sign in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV LHCb. With an gathered data integral of 2 fb$^{-1}$, the standard model prediction of the background was independently determined. A significance of 4.0 $\sigma$ for the desired outcome was discovered, using 107 unconfirmed decays, corresponding to 0.10 percentage of $\Sigma^+ $ decay. After adjusting for the predicted number of $\Sigma^+ $ events, the latter result equivalent to $4.4\times 10^{-4}$ or 1.3 standard model predicted $\Sigma^+ $ decay. No indication was discovered for non-standard longitudinal muon spin asymmetry, but rather consistent with the standard model prediction of no colour exchange during this process.

The beginning of the solar nebula and planetary accretion is thought to originate from the gravitational collapse of prestellar cores. However, the conventional view of a smooth, prestellar core collapse needing thousands of years, for planet formation to commence, is challenged by a new model. This model proposes that the solar nebula and planets could form in a few thousand years as a result of the core collapse breaking up into protostellar disks. In this study, a case is examined where a core collapses into a spiral, protostellar disk. In this scenario, a central, gas-free core forms and subsequently experiences break-ups, producing small-scale, solid matter protoplanetary disks. In about 2.8 years, the core dissipates, with material from the core accreted by nearby particles. In this scenario, large-scale, gas-rich disks take significantly longer to develop, with most gas-free cores in these disks needing thousands of years to collapse. As a result, it is possible that the formation of planets from the breakdown of a prestellar core material is the primary mechanism for their formation.

A new model for atmospheric dispersion that has been analyzed from observational data on the sky exhibits complex characteristics, with variations that depend on atmospheric altitude. This behavior matches the shape of a function composed of polynomials of degrees 6 and below, although the highest dispersion occurs at an altitude of about 5 km. Factors like atmospheric temperature, humidity, and wind influence this phenomenon. To improve optical telescope accuracy, data on atmospheric dispersion across various wavelengths have been collected from observation decks. Least squares fitting techniques have been applied to this information to develop mathematical equations describing atmospheric dispersion patterns at different elevations. These models, which account for humidity and pressure levels at the Earth's surface, have been formulated into a practical solution that can be implemented in real-world applications.

This paper employs a refined mixture of allowing for varying numbers of components in each category, using the mixture of normal distributions as an example. The traditional Bayesian approach to such models relies on the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method for estimation, which faces issues due to selected starting points and potential unexplored regions. To address these limitations, a refined approach using Bayesian variational inference is proposed, which guarantees convergence to the model's equilibrium. The efficiency of the new model is showcased through a significant reduction in computational time compared to the traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo method in empirical tests. The model's performance is further demonstrated through successful predictions and qualitative analysis in diverse real-world data contexts, including yield simulation, inflation rate forecasting, and extreme event detection.

We discover models of monadic first-order constant logic that serve as Stone duality spaces for local groups. Furthermore, through the application of Stone duality and Pontryagin duality, it can be demonstrated that the class of definalisable sets within a Stone space correlates with the class of profinite groups having a subspace homeomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.

The rapid advancement of wireless technologies, particularly 5G, has led to an explosive growth in the use of IoT devices, which have further fueled the interest in developing innovative machine learning approaches that are both efficient and secure. To counter the unfavorable conditions that may compromise the integrity of trained models, such as data heterogeneity and privacy concerns, researchers have been working on adapting existing machine learning techniques to the fluctuating environments characteristic of wireless networks. Specifically, federated learning, an innovative federated learning paradigm, allows participants to train models on their local data while avoiding data exchange, which addresses concerns related to data privacy. Despite these advancements, there are still pressing challenges to address, such as ensuring fairness in the training process to guarantee that all participants contribute equally to model development. Since implementing fairness measures on top of existing FL architectures can be complex, researchers require a thorough understanding of the interplay between FL and fairness. Additionally, to protect the privacy of client data despite the robust nature of FL, which allows for robust model training even with moderate data corruption, single-layer neural networks are particularly vulnerable to information leakage, which necessitates a more robust FL framework that can guarantee the protection of client data despite the training process. To address these challenges, this paper offers a comprehensive overview of the application of a pioneering PL framework that can guarantee privacy without compromise, accompanied by an in-depth analysis of the interplay between FL and fairness, including the latest advancements in fairness for FL, which focuses on the protection of client data.

The Supersymmetric Standard Extension model, featuring a novel $U(1)_X$ gauge group where $B-W$-like neutral gauge bosons reside, has been created. Within this model, supermultiparts are paired with each other, then a right-handed neutrino is introduced and it is demonstrated that this model is naturally in a state of $Z_2$ dark matter symmetry due to the presence of both Standard Model and $U(1)_X$ gauged $R$-symmetries. As a result, the dark matter particles are stable and indistinguishable from Standard Model supermultiparts. Furthermore, the presence of $U(1)_X$ gauge group generates an abundance of dark matter in the early universe, rendering the need for $moduli$ or other factors to induce the formation of dark matter obsolete. This model's characteristic features comprise of a moderately sized $mu$ parameter, $h_{eff}$, and a relatively small ratio of $v_s^2$ to $v_{1}^2$, which together enable the model to satisfy the constraints imposed by Higgs inflation while restricting the model's parameter space. Additionally, the model's particle content, particularly the dark matter and $U(1)_X$ gauge group, along with neutrino presence, generates a $7.85 x 10^5$ year age for the universe which matches with the currently accepted age of $13.8$ billion years for the universe

A single intelligent surface-assisted wireless-powered downlink network is investigated where the energy harvesting user equipment receives transmissions from multiple energy sources over a multi-path fading channel simultaneously. The sources' transmission powers are initially optimized to maximize the energy harvesting rate at the user equipment, while subsequently, the intelligent surface's phase shift matrix is optimized to minimize interference at the other users. The resulting problem, however, is shown to be a non-convex problem due to the involvement of the variable phase shifts in the expressions for interference power. A major contribution of this paper is to introduce an unsupervised learning approach to tackle this issue. A key component of this approach is to transform the problem into a continuous form by approximating discrete phase shifts with real-valued functions, thus simplifying the problem. Another contribution of this paper is to propose a novel deep autoencoder model to solve the resulting problem, which is both computationally efficient and unsupervised. The paper also presents an alternative approach to test the efficacy of the proposed approach using a genetic algorithm with a modified binary formulation. Numerical results show the efficacy and accuracy of the proposed solution.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au and compared it to theoretical QRPA calculations employing the SLy4 Skyrme force. The measured strength distribution, alongside the nuclei's half-lives, is best explained by incorporating a combination of prolate and oblate configurations independently in the parent and daughter nuclei. Prolate components dominated both parent and daughter nuclei for the experimental beta strength, while an upper limit was placed on the oblate component in the parent state. To analyze the data, a new method for examining X-ray gated total absorption spectra was developed due to the analysis's complexity.

Within the framework of the unified gauge theories, a novel mechanism of neutrinoless $\beta$ decay emerges when dark matter particles interact with lepton and dark fields. The latter's interaction breaks lepton number, while the former's interaction with lepton number affects baryogenesis and lepton number anomaly in the universe. Furthermore, dark matter particles' decay into inert particles may lead to significant leptogenesis. This research investigates how these processes interplay under a common framework, emphasizing their connections to the masses of neutrinos and related cosmological signs.

In a control system with limited data and no demonstrations, we employ side information to achieve our objectives. Specifically, we demonstrate a novel approach that combines dynamic modeling and control, leveraging this method with different forms of side information to effectively control nonlinear systems, even those with unpredictable dynamics. We begin by developing a neural network-based model that accurately predicts future system behavior based on past observations, utilizing this method with various types of system trajectory data. Next, we create a controller by optimizing a predicted system trajectory that meets our objectives, doing so efficiently by using an iterative method to update system parameters and trajectory settings. We then test the effectiveness of this method with simulated systems mimicking a quadrotor, a snake, and a human gait, even when the initial data and system dynamics are unknown.

Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a simple Lie algebra, and let $\mathcal{W}$ be the associated Toda conformal field theory developed by Feigin and Reshetikhin in the early 1990s. This talk focuses on the ward identities within the $\mathcal{W}$-algebra for the specific case where the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is equal to $\mathfrak{sl}_3$. It was discovered that these identities come in a hierarchical structure, and that a decomposition of the complete set of these identities into lower-level components, each corresponding to a unitary representation of the associated Lie algebra, results in the emergence of the associated affine Gaudin model and the degenerate $\mathcal{W}$-algebra associated with a full Weyl partition, respectively. This talk extends prior work initially presented in arXiv:2106.11727, specifically considering the scenario where the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ supports four non-zero non-zero simple roots.

Despite the outstanding performance of Relation Networks (R- Networks) in various applications, its integration with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains largely unexplored. This study seeks to bridge this knowledge gap by developing novel RNET-based GAN architectures on two challenging datasets, ImageNet and CIFAR, and demonstrating the efficacy of a modified triplet loss in these models. The proposed architectures, featuring a superior ability to match discriminative capabilities, have been found to surpass the existing state-of-the-art in multiple metrics, while a notable improvement in image quality has been observed particularly in the evaluation of FID score.

We have successfully achieved quantum key exchange without the need for phase locking within a twin-field setup, which would typically require this step but hasn't been feasible in practice. By adopting an alternative approach utilizing distinct phase detection methods, we've devised two methods to accomplish this. The first method utilizes directly detected twin-field quantum key exchange, while the second builds upon entanglement-based twin-field key exchange and involves post-processing the results to eliminate locking issues. In our experiments, we've demonstrated both approaches with notable performance results, including an impressive key rate of 0.573 random bits per pulse when using the direct approach, and a key rate of 0.411 random bits per pulse when using the entanglement-based approach. These achievements represent significant progress towards fully functional QKD over long distances without the necessity of phase locking.

In this study, we investigate the Toeplitz algebra with respect to a symbol class consisting of bounded, complex-valued functions defined on the complex plane. The Toeplitz algebra $T_{\alpha}^p$ is specifically considered for Fock space $F_p^N$ and Hardy space $H^N$, both weighted by the $N$-variable Gaussian measure $\alpha$, yielding a characterization of its norm closure in terms of a norm that relies on the $L^q$ norm of symbols for a specific $q$. The found value of $q$ can be extended to the limit case of $p=1$, indicating the existence of a continuous linear mapping from $M_{m \times m}(F_p^N,\alpha)$ to $M_{m \times m}(F_1^N,\alpha)$ that sends the Toeplitz algebra to the maximal Toeplitz algebra. Additionally, our results can be complemented with an exploration of Toeplitz operators' representability, both as Toeplitz operators and in a larger class of multipliers, in relation to the Volterra operator, the shift operator, and weighted Bergman spaces.

In object identification within image datasets, object categories and their spatial locations are closely linked. Finite category lists, however, limit the potential for object identification systems to adapt and grow. To address this limitation, our research presents a novel approach to object identification known as PseudoLabel-BBox (PL-Bbox), which assigns precise coordinate labels to finite category datasets. By designing a novel framework combining a feature extractor, a classifier, and a coordinate predictor, our approach can generate high-quality coordinate labels through a self-supervised process. These derived coordinates, in turn, enhance the performance of the object identification system as a whole. To validate the effectiveness of PL-Bbox, we applied it to the development of a state-of-the-art system for identifying the seven fundamental object categories and achieved results equivalent to recent high-tech models tailored to specific object categories. Furthermore, our approach successfully predicted the coordinates of all object categories within the COCO dataset with remarkable accuracy.

The shape and dimensions of photochemical recombination regions in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud, surrounding a bright young star, have been investigated based on the reanalysis of previous H2 maps as well as related data on carbon monoxide, CCS, and formaldehyde. The photochemical recombination regions in the cloud surrounding the star exhibit a distinctive 'bowl' shape, which can be modeled using an axisymmetric, flared geometry. Measurements indicate that the cloud surrounding the star begins approximately 20,000 AU in diameter and rises 8,000 AU above the plane of the solar system. An alternative model that takes into account the complex structure of the cloud results in similar dimensions. Unsettlingly, the sum of the gas and dust masses in the photochemical recombination regions cannot account for the star's continued supply of material, which must be provided through a wind. This discovery is in contrast to the star Rho Ophiuchus b which also displays an excess in the excess in the excess in the optical depth but does not have an accretion excess. Furthermore, the star Rho Ophiuchus a which also does not have an optical excess in the optical and near infrared ranges.

Deep learning's prominent model, the Transformer, has gained significant attention. Initially, it was employed in text-based domains such as machine translation and text classification but has since been adapted for various image and audio-related tasks. One of the key motivations behind its development was its ability to overcome traditional recurrent neural network limitations. Following its emergence, the Transformer has been subjected to rigorous testing, with its potential beyond data-driven tasks being explored. This includes its capability to process data in a graph-based setting. This paper aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the graph-based setting of the Transformer, specifically focusing on its applications and graph node/edge generation methods. It will also discuss associated challenges and future research directions.

The purpose of this paper is to create a precise prediction model for social care, which is based on the needs assessment of elderly individuals and their related families. This model uses factor regression, an approach developed by shareable variable sets, to identify essential factors in data captured from sensor readings, patient health records, and other sources. These variable sets can be accessed online at https://github.com/smartcare-fp7/generic-datasets. Initially, we analyze how factor loadings change over time within data sets from three diverse sources. Our findings suggest that factor regression performance is more consistent when factor representations do not evolve over time. Consequently, we created a time-invariant method for updating factor representations, which is based on principal component analysis with fixed dimensionality. Our experiments using real and simulated data indicate that this approach produces accurate predictions. Moreover, we utilize Bayesian methods to identify optimal weighting strategies for combining the predictions from multiple, independently trained models. Our results show that factor regression is a valuable machine learning technique with significant potential in the context of healthcare, particularly for developing accurate models that can inform decision-making and decision-support systems.

The objective of neural architecture search (NAS) is to automate the design of
architectures that perform well on task-specific datasets. Consequently, there
has been growing interest in identifying remaining constraints that impede
NAS's full potential. In this research, we explore how interference affects NAS,
specifically when samples from external sources influence outcomes in NAS
experiments. We analyze the impact of interference on NAS performance and
investigate whether existing NAS models can account for this phenomenon. We
then design and evaluate a novel NAS model that mitigates interference and
outperforms current models. We also examine whether our proposed model can
generalize its performance to task-space and demonstrate its effectiveness on
different datasets. Overall, our study sheds light on NAS performance degradation
due to interference and showcases the potential of leveraging theoretical NAS
models to address this issue.

Time series data in various fields are analyzed to gain insights into trends over time. Comparing multiple time series often requires goalseeking to establish baselines for assessing performance. For instance, a company may aim to outperform the market as a whole. In such cases, surfacing key characteristics of the comparison time series is essential. Frequently, these attributes encompass trends, magnitudes, volatility, and correlations. Revealing these features can augment the interpretation of the resulting time series forecasts or classifications and inform decision-making about optimization strategies or evaluation metrics. Existing methodologies in the R ecosystem focus either on measuring one metric at a time or are too basic for advanced goal-oriented optimization. Consequently, there is a gap for methodologies in R that can accurately and efficiently extract essential features from time series to support informed, goal-oriented decision-making. This paper introduces the theft package in R, which uses both basic and advanced techniques to provide essential time series features. The package includes functions for 13 basic attributes and 16 advanced attributes, offering flexibility through two different data types. The package is accompanied by examples and demonstrations of its capabilities, including a case study of the NYSE during the COVID-19 pandemic to illustrate its utility in uncovering time series patterns.

This research focuses on the topological properties of geometric borders within the framework of CAT(0) spaces. A new classification system, termed 'geodesic completeness', is established to describe the behavior of geodesics on the boundary of 2-dimensional CAT(0) spaces. It is demonstrated that the concept of relative hyperbolicity is closely related to this boundary model. The following key results are achieved: (1) a non-elementary hyperbolic 3-manifold's boundary is geodesically complete, (2) a certain type of space called 'thin CAT(0)' can be identified with the boundary of a 2-dimensional CAT(0) space that is geodesically complete, and (3) a measure of the boundary's 'thickness' is defined and the following identity is established: the thickness of the boundary of a 2-dimensional CAT(0) space that is geodesically complete corresponds to the hyperbolicity convergence exponent of its fundamental group.

Human-assisted translation, which involves translators, is sometimes imperfect and can introduce errors, affecting the quality of the translation. To address this, a quantitative framework is developed to evaluate the translation skills of human assistants using several forms of annotation. This involves examining various types of proof, including explicit feedback, implicit suggestions, and self-assessment, all of which are treated equally as probabilistic indicators of translation accuracy. A system is put in place to combine the different types of evidence and determine their reliability. Afterward, a system is introduced that integrates this process, utilizing feedback from multiple translators, and identifies the most trustworthy translators for a specific subject matter. Lastly, a system is developed that incorporates the translation skills of all translators and ensures the quality of the translation.

Recent studies have introduced energy eigenstates as a valid basis for describing energy transport in disordered systems, distinct from traditional statistical approaches. Building upon this work, we derive mathematical expressions for total and differential sums of energy eigenstate coefficients in both discrete and continuous domains. Our findings demonstrate that these sums can be linked to eigenstate correlations and provide insights into the statistical properties of eigenstates. While certain total sum values appear to follow a non-intuitive pattern, further analysis reveals that differential sums exhibit more consistent behavior and are ultimately governed by fundamental principles. These principles also apply to eigenstates derived from related "null channels." We conclude by exploring the implications of our work in the context of experimental systems, including quantum dynamics and energy storage and transfer in photonic systems, as well as possible extensions to more complex systems.

The concept of "lottery ticket theory" has enabled researchers to identify and analyze the crucial subsets within large neural networks. Through a series of experiments, we evaluated the theory's applicability to fully connected layers by finding the optimal subset size for different training periods on different datasets, including MNIST, SVHN, and EMNIST. Notably, for the first time, we discovered the optimal subset size for wide neural networks on MNIST to be significantly smaller than the entire network, at just 1.8% of parameters, when trained for 300 epochs. Interestingly, similar results were found when using other training epochs, suggesting a distinct pattern. Unlike previous research on convolutional layers, our findings indicate that the best-performing subset of fully connected layers has an surprisingly small size, close to 1%, shedding new light on the theory's initial predictions. Moreover, our analysis of the significant errors made by the best-subset selection process revealed a pattern where misclassifications often occur in categories that are similar to each other, paving the way for future work to explore ensemble methods that utilize diverse, smaller sub-networks to mitigate this issue.

The concept of anticipated utility theory is typically applied to describe how people make decisions about risks in their daily lives, but it's often disputed whether or not individuals behave according to this paradigm. Despite the existence of methods such as value-of-information metrics that quantify risk-taking through the anticipated value of information, this theory remains underutilized in the field of machine learning. In our research, we examine how the anticipated value of a training dataset impacts the performance of sparsification techniques, particularly in the context of residual connection-based neural networks. By utilizing the anticipated utility of a loss as a measurement of dataset value, and combining it with a training strategy involving pseudo-labels and dynamic threshold adjustment, we achieve exceptional results on residual connection-free and residual-connection-based handwrite classification and residual-connection-based datasets, notably outperforming existing methods. Notably, this approach successfully identifies the optimal level of dataset utilization and avoids overfitting, while its anticipated value of a training dataset also correlates with expected generalization performance. Additionally, this method is uniquely positioned to handle big datasets without needing to introduce regularization, and its efficiency is further highlighted by its ability to locate an optimal subset of the training dataset in a relatively short amount of time.

The value of the six-loop anomaly exponent of the $O(N)$ symmetric model's $\phi^Q$ operator has been determined for $Q \leq 3$, specifically for the $O(N)$ symmetric model and its $O(Q)$ subgroup. This was done by analyzing the critical properties of the $O(N)$ linear sigma model in the six-loop calculations. Within the $O(N)$ symmetry, the $\phi^Q$ operator's dimension is given by $|Q| + (2 \beta_{\phi^Q}/3)_5$, whereas in the $O(Q)$ subgroup, it's given by $Q + (2 \lambda_{\phi^Q}/3)_5$, with the subscripts denoting the results of the five-loop and six-loop calculations, respectively. These new results have allowed for the refinement of previous estimates of the critical properties of the $O(N)$ linear sigma model. Notably, the six-loop calculations have provided the value of $\lambda_{\phi^3}/\lambda_{\phi^1}$, yielding $(2 \lambda_{\phi^3}/3 \lambda_{\phi^1})_5 = 1.07617(17)$, and helped to determine the generalization of the Konig-Tuynman-Wysocki-Wysocki-Mouhou-Shaikh-Jamaev-Anikin estimate for the $\beta$-function's leading six-loop component. Recent studies on a particular type of material, called a 2D monolayer transition metal dichalcogenide, have exposed the role of electron-phonon coupling (EPC) in generating intervalley transitions. This process can be broken down into three mechanisms: the change in shape effect, the tilt of boundaries effect, and the scattering within the orbit. This research has developed a computational model to study these phenomena within a particular type of transition metal dichalcogenide, producing results which accurately correlate with available experimental data. Analysis indicates that the combination of two specific types of transitions, known as intervalley transitions, contribute equally to suppressing a particular type of transition, known as valley Hall effect. This finding raises questions about the validity of previous theories which attributed this effect to single type of transition, known as intervalley transition, and highlights the need to reconsider these theories.

We accomplished the first-ever completion of the VisDA challenge by winning
the top spot in the leaderboards for both unsupervised domain adaptation and
domain generalization tasks. Our approach leverages a dual training strategy
that initially uses an iterative process to generate synthetic target-domain
training data, starting with the provided target domain test images, and
then adapts feature representations to the target domain using a joint
distribution of source and target domain data. Additionally, for VisDA-specific rules, we implemented a method to enforce label alignment during the adaptation process. Furthermore, we developed a domain generalization approach by aggregating features from multiple datasets and then applying it to the test domain. Our method's accuracy on the VisDA 2017 dataset is 69.10%, securing our first-place finish in the challenge.

Non-Euclidean data such as points on a sphere or projective space cannot be effectively embedded in a linear space like Euclidean data. The t-SNE algorithm is popular for visualizing complex data but struggles with spherical distributions, often producing unreliable results. We developed a spherical variant of t-SNE, specifically tailored to handle spherical data constraints while maintaining compatibility with the original method. Our approach provides reliable results and yields consistent outcomes compared to the standard t-SNE method. Furthermore, we applied the same framework to develop a probabilistic clustering method for spherical data. This technique performs clustering in a probabilistic setting and offers a measure of classification accuracy, along with predicted cluster labels.

We apply the innovative concept of strain in experimental quantum chemistry to the study of a Fermi polaron in two-dimensional systems, leveraging the power of diagrammatic Monte Carlo calculations to explore the interaction between a heavy particle and a Fermi sea. Our method reveals the impact of high-order diagrams containing multiple loops, which significantly enhances the accuracy in this context. When adjusting the strength of interaction, we observe the development of exciton-like quasiparticles, known as polarons, that deviate from the predicted linear-liquids model. Extensive analysis of our results indicates that the character of polarons depends on the interplay between the scattering length, the effective repulsive potential, and the number of available Fermi sea particles. Furthermore, we identify a phenomenon where the interaction between the polaron and the Fermi sea particles exhibits multiple solutions, which is explored using both variational principles and self-consistent approaches. Our research demonstrates that the two-dimensional Fermi polaron exhibits behaviors that are distinct from those observed in one-dimensional systems and budrons, thereby revealing intricate social interactions within the former.

Recent advancements in quantum computing have led to increased interest in developing emulators for complex quantum systems, particularly those with an infinite number of variables like fermionic systems. These systems are particularly challenging due to their unique characteristics, such as non-abelian order and intricate interplay between local and non-local degrees of freedom. Traditional simulations using coupler-qubit gates are restricted to specific fermionic configurations, like half-filled states, thanks to their anti-linear character. However, a new approach to quantum computing, known as the hybrid digital-analog protocol, offers a more efficient way to simulate fermionic systems with the help of a quantum computer. This protocol enables the simulation of fermionic states with specific fermion counts as well as interactions between different subspaces, all within a reasonable number of qubits and quantum gates. We outline a quantum algorithm that can implement this protocol to achieve this goal and analyze its performance based on current quantum computing technology. Furthermore, our discussion on potential applications focuses on their relevance to one-dimensional quantum liquids and the simulation of topological fermionic states.

This article examines several families of polynomials derived from the invariants of graph connections and evaluates the potential for each family to produce an complete set of graph invariants by analyzing the rings formed by these polynomials and their connections to specific graph characteristics. Graph connections and their associated polynomials are defined as collections of graphs generated by a specific transformation process. Several distinct types of these connections, which yield equivalent rings of polynomials, are studied along with the rings formed by complete graph connections and subconnections, which cannot yield an complete set of graph invariants. However, it is discovered that the ring of polynomials derived from oriented complete graph connections does provide an complete set of graph invariants. These findings also reveal a link between the Euler characteristic of a particular graph and its curvature, which is defined as the alternating sum of the numbers of edges in each graph degradation level.

We demonstrate the Hitchin moduli space lies on a Veech curve for curves of genus 2 and 3, utilizing 2009's techniques from Borel's free case, and extend the method from Li and Zarhin for genus 3 to all hyperelliptic curves of higher genus.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, multiple countries imposed lockdowns resulting in a widespread shift of up to 90% of employees working remotely. As a consequence, numerous businesses were forced to adopt hybrid or fully remote project management methods. Though successful, many companies struggled to navigate the challenges associated with working from home, prompting an investigation into its impact on project success. Our study examines the influence of working from home on the success of Scrum projects using a multi-method approach. First, a quantitative survey of 226 professionals working from home provided insights into the benefits and drawbacks of this arrangement. Next, a qualitative interview with 20 companies identified both the obstacles they faced and potential strategies for working from home to achieve Scrum's principles. Our analysis indicates that working from home poses risks to Scrum projects, led by the absence of clear boundaries between work and personal life. As working from home becomes more common, businesses must develop effective policies to mitigate these challenges, ultimately enabling remote teams to excel. Our research sheds light on the key factors for working from home to achieve Scrum's principles, guiding companies and practitioners working remotely to achieve project success.

This research introduces an approach to calculating the Gau-Wu value of arrowhead matrices with dimensions of 4x4. Additionally, we derive general expressions for the Gau-Wu value of 4x4 Hermitian matrices and the Gau-Wu sign of these matrices. We also examine the Gau-Wu value and sign of 4x4 skew-Hermitian matrices. Either numerical or graphical methods can be employed to determine these values, depending on the form of the matrix's elements. Relevantly, these calculations are applicable to a broad spectrum of real-world problems involving the representation of non-axisymmetric three-dimensional objects.

In a study using the ALICE detector at the LHC, scientists investigated the elliptical movement of electrons resulting from the decay of charm and beauty particles created in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions. The results show that these electrons, with masses less than approximately 3 GeV, exhibit significant elliptical movement. The research found that a particular model, assuming certain conditions and properties of charm and beauty particles, can accurately account for observed data across different collision energies. The results support earlier findings and suggest that the elliptical movement of charm and beauty particles is consistent with predictions related to the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. The research also provides new insights, with data analysis showing that the average lifetime of charm and beauty particles is consistent with predictions in certain conditions near the surface of the quark-gluon plasma, but this finding is limited by current detector capabilities.

In topological data analysis, the key challenge is often to uncover complex patterns hidden in data, which is a difficult task. The techniques developed in this research are aimed at addressing this problem: introducing novel topological methods for dimensionality reduction, classification, and clustering. The underlying idea is based on the concept of $k$-chromatic alpha structures - a representation of permuted spaces that takes into account color information. The reduced life-line of these structures provides a compressed representation of their topology. Furthermore, we establish conditions under which their reduced life-line determines the original configuration of the points. Additionally, we demonstrate applications of these structures in performing $k$-clustering on datasets and developing classification models based on multi-layer neural networks.

This work presents new results for the optimal rate of convergence in groups of users sharing frequencies with multiple levels of signal attenuation. When there are an even number of groups, we find the general form of this convergence rate to be approximately proportional to $2^{-\frac{1-\mu_K}{2}\sqrt{K}}$, where the exponent depends on the mutual information definition used and a function $\mu_K$ that varies with the number of groups, while for groups of odd numbers, we find the convergence rate to be approximately proportional to $2^{-\frac{1-\mu_K}{2}\sqrt{K}}$ plus an arbitrary small value. It has also been confirmed that this convergence rate cannot be surpassed by any other possible power control methods. To investigate this issue further, we have also derived the achievable rates for signals with binary, linear and Gaussian powers in a multi-user environment with multiple frequencies. These findings were then used to determine the optimal power control method which in turn was then utilized in an analysis of a multi-user environment with an even number of groups to find the optimal achievable rate. It has been observed that for a given number of frequencies N, as the number of groups K increases without bound, the optimal achievable rate for signals with binary, linear and Gaussian powers converge to the same value. A novel, computationally efficient algorithm has been developed that utilizes Markov chain Monte Carlo methods to simulate the Strauss point process. Based on the fundamental idea of "stitching," this approach divides a two-dimensional space into smaller, separable regions where the density of points can be efficiently simulated. By applying this concept, the simulation time for the Strauss process has been significantly reduced, achieving a scale-up factor proportional to the square root of the number of regions. Empirical studies demonstrating this advancement have been conducted using two-dimensional spaces of sizes 128x128 and 256x256.

In the context of string theory and quantum gravity, the generalized uncertainty principle led to modifications in momentum space, which were previously demonstrated to incorporate a minimum momentum, proportional to the Planck momentum. This work builds on those findings by examining their effects on Lorentz and Galilean transformations. Building on the generalized transformation for momentum, the authors propose a new form for the Lorentz and Galilean transformations, which conserves their respective commutative properties. Interestingly, the proposed transformations exhibit deviations that become more pronounced at high momentum values, departing from their classical forms. This work also explores the implications of these transformations on quantum field theory and the speed of light.

We consider a situation in which a service unit receives a constant stream of requests for multiple tasks and uses a fixed amount of time to complete each request from a pooled group. To optimize average wait times, a policy known as "order-independent allocation" consistently assigns tasks in the same proportion to each unit. When units work at a constant rate, this policy results in the lowest average wait times. Order-independent allocation is straightforward to implement in situations where tasks are processed at an average rate. This paper examines the scenario where units work at varying rates. We show that while achieving the lowest average wait times may be possible, it often requires a more complex reallocation policy that takes into account the speed of each unit. In some instances, even order-independent allocation results in the lowest average wait times even when applied consistently. However, in other instances, the best outcome can only be achieved with a dynamic reallocation policy based on unit speed. In addition, we found that while faster units should handle more tasks in a system with order-independent allocation, this is not always the case in other pooled allocation mechanisms. In fact, even when all units have different speeds, the only situation in which faster units handle more tasks in all other pooled allocation mechanisms is when they work at varying rates in order-independent allocation. This result is unique because it doesn't occur in other pooled allocation mechanisms, situations in which tasks are processed at an average rate, or cases in which units either have the same speed or no speed is present.

This research explores how a single-legged robot moves by hopping over soft ground through both theoretical modeling and simulation, as well as an analysis of potential enhancements to its design. To study its movement, we used the rigid body dynamics simulation tool, Track3D. To simulate the effect of the ground's softness, we used the Voronoi finite difference method to create a continuous and non-linear terrain model that allows the robot's legs to penetrate into it. Based on this simulation, we developed a theoretical model of the robot's motion by simplifying its movement and considering the ground as a spring, which helped us understand how the ground's softness affects its behavior. Furthermore, we used this understanding to simulate and analyze the robot's movement under different conditions, such as varying its mass, leg stiffness, and ground elasticity, all while keeping its actuator force constant. This allowed us to identify the trade-offs between these modifications and the robot's ability to hop, as well as how these modifications could be used to make the robot's movement more stable and robust by adjusting its design parameters.

In recent years, deploying reliable software updates on large-scale IoT networks has gained significant attention, especially due to the security implications involved. Various studies have proposed different approaches, such as using the CoAP protocol and mesh networks, to enhance the efficiency and dependability of update mechanisms. Despite the prominence of these topics, there is a noticeable shortage of comprehensive studies in this area. To bridge this knowledge gap, our research contributes to this field by exploring the performance of IoT firmware updates. By designing, testing, and evaluating a large-scale IoT network with 64 nodes, we examined how different configuration settings, protocol versions, and optimization techniques affect the efficiency and reliability of update deployment. The outcome of our investigation not only sheds light on the performance of IoT firmware updates but also provides invaluable insights that can inform similar experiments, allowing researchers and practitioners to replicate our findings and apply them to real-world problems.

We investigate the behavior of multifractal spectra in one-dimensional localized, non-Gaussian many-body systems that transition from localized to delocalized phases. Our study involves analyzing the fractal dimensions of the Fock space propagation, as obtained from high-order polynomials that approximate the multi-body Schrödinger equation. Through this, we demonstrate that the system exhibits distinct fractal behaviors on either side of the many-body localization phase transition, with the extent of this deviation increasing as the polynomial order diminishes. Conversely, when the system is in a state of many-body localization, it displays multifractal characteristics with a "U" shaped spectrum, which meets certain fractal dimension bounds, with the exception of a zero-dimensional point at the middle of the spectrum. Conversely, outside of this phase of many-body localization, the multifractal spectrum exhibits negative fractal dimensions for energies near the middle. These findings are further validated with the many-body Schrödinger equation and the Nash inequality. Our study also shows that the system displays distinct phases in the disorder $\phi$ with the exception of a second-order phase transition at $\phi_c$. Our results indicate that the shift from localized to delocalized phases in many-body localization exhibits distinct fractal properties with the exception of a zero-dimensional point at $\phi_c$.
