Directed spaces, initially developed as an algebraic counterpart to ordered sets, have undergone expansion into the category of directed spaces, consisting of sets equipped with partial orders. This work defines topological spaces with this partial order as part of the power framework, then explores their relationship with spaces having a preorder structure. It also establishes connections between well-ordered spaces and various classes of directed spaces, using the power framework. This investigation, resulting in numerous properties and examples, serves as a comprehensive continuation of directed space theory, providing a foundational approach with the properties of preorders intact.

Future climate models indicate that intense downpours are likely to become more severe due to climate change, and the effect is already being felt on a planet similar to Earth. Our research, which involved analyzing weather patterns on Mars with a climate model, shows that we can expect significant precipitation once the threshold of 0.7 kW/m^2 is exceeded. Once this threshold is reached, downpours of large amounts - ranging from 1-100 mm per hour - become much more frequent and frequent, and the elevation of the terrain has a major impact on where these downpours occur. As a result, we expect to see frequent flooding in low-lying areas, and the elevation of the terrain plays a major role in determining where and how these downpours form.

We've developed an innovative twistor construction for a broad range of Yang-Mills theories with higher-dimensional components and self-dual properties. The general case relies on novel higher-valuation meromorphic forms on the twistor space. The solution to a related higher-differential analog of the Cauchy integral formula enables us to break down the Yang-Mills equations into simpler components. We've also discovered that our twistor formulation applies not only to Yang-Mills theories but also to more complex self-dual theories with higher-dimensional components. Although we've adapted the traditional twistor construction to incorporate higher-spin properties, this modification imposes specific constraints on the theory's structure, effectively limiting it to a specific class of higher-spin generalizations of self-dual Yang-Mills theory.

The use of deep learning in medical image classification has experienced significant advancements, with its applications extending to addressing various complex medical issues. Despite its potential, this approach is heavily reliant on accurate labels, which can often be inadvertently compromised during the data collection process. Consequently, implementing AIC-based noise mitigation to alleviate the adverse effects of label noise is becoming increasingly crucial. In order to mitigate label noise through the augmentation of the training dataset, we initially determine the likelihood of a label being accurate (termed 'credit') by analyzing the behavior of the training data. We then propose an iterative process where we identify and correct noisy labels by considering the 'credit' value and other factors, taking into account the behavior of the entire dataset. We have successfully implemented this method, which we call the 'BLR' algorithm, and evaluated its effectiveness through comparisons with established noise mitigation techniques using publicly accessible medical image classification datasets. The results obtained from this comparison study reveal that the BLR algorithm is capable of delivering superior performance while also being computationally efficient.

This article provides fresh estimates for the norm of a projector that results from multivariate interpolation using linearly separated evaluations of a function. These estimates are specifically tailored to the thin-grid interpolation case.

A degenerate stochastic matrix derived from a graph's adjacency matrix is used to analyze random walks that are prohibited from visiting certain vertices. Let's denote this matrix by $\mathbf{P}$. The eigenvalues of $\mathbf{P}$, along with their associated eigenvectors, are determined through a maximal common divisor calculation with the graph's adjacency matrix $\mathbf{A}$. This calculation is further generalized to graphs that are either connected or disconnected. The eigenvalue decomposition of $\mathbf{P}$ can also be extended to all connected graphs and weighted graphs, with a final application in the analysis of directed graphs that contain cycles.

In this work, we establish a fundamental understanding of time and its function within the logical framework of HOL, building upon the fundamental logic principles.  Time is identified as advancing in a consistent and uniform manner.  Initially, we establish the concept of a point in time, represented as a real number.  Subsequently, we define a function that links times to their descriptions, characterized as the passage of a unit of time.  Additionally, we define a family of sets that encompasses all possible states at a given time.  This fundamental structure enables the generation of a timed automaton, capable of accurately modeling systems that progress over time.

A new, data-driven method has been created to enhance the predictions made by a type of model called the attached eddy model (AEM), which helps to generate synthetic data that can be used to refine the understanding of wall-bounded turbulence. This new method, called the optimized AEM, is based on a type of machine learning algorithm and uses the results from high-resolution simulations of turbulent flow to generate synthetic data. When tested using high-resolution simulations of turbulent flow in different types of channels, the optimized AEM was found to provide more accurate predictions of the flow's complexity and variability compared to the original version, with results that are remarkably similar to those from the high-resolution simulations. This new method has the potential to provide a more complete understanding of the flow's complexity and variability, with the ability to be applied to different types of channels and with lower computational requirements.

This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons in a newly formed model by combining the Skyrme model with modified infant versions of the Born-Infeld Maxwell equations. The work involves analyzing a real-time Skyrme model accompanied by a non-linear electromagnetic field component. The model is formulated in a 4D Minkowski spacetime setting. The work includes a detailed review of the underlying mathematical structure, specifically the static configurations of the solitons. This review reveals the necessary conditions required for the existence of these solitons in the model. The work concludes with a presentation of examples that display the geometric properties associated with topological non-trivial configurations of the solitons.

By numerically solving the Bethe-Salpeter equation for two fermions with different charges and hoppings in a square lattice under a magnetic field, we studied the relationship between the magnetic flux and spectral properties for both time-reversal and time-reversal-breaking cases. For the first scenario, we observed the appearance of chiral edge modes only for certain integer multiples of magnetic flux. In contrast, the second scenario exhibited more general results, with the edge modes depending on both the magnetic flux's integer part and its fractional part. The observed edge modes satisfied all conditions of Weyl fermions, earning the studied regime the title of a time-reversal-broken Weyl metal. The time-reversal-broken scenario's stability was confirmed through its resilience to perturbations. Moreover, we outlined a general method to determine whether a given edge spectrum is from a chiral or Weyl type, which does not rely on edge density of states calculations.

The interplay between plasmon-assisted emission and radiation from two-dimensional nanoantennas has significant implications for the generation of entangled and bright photon sources. This study presents a numerical model for analyzing the optical properties of a specific nanoantenna consisting of a resonant metal island coupled to an emitting point source via a thin dielectric wall. The insights gained from this model can be applied to explore a wider range of hybrid nanoantenna designs that combine the advantages of both plasmonic and dielectric scattering mechanisms. The simulations demonstrate how various photonic emissions, including plasmonic-enhanced, radiative, and scattering patterns, can be generated by manipulating the proximity of the emitter to the metal island and the size of the gap between them. Furthermore, changing the polarization of the light emitted by the island reveals the efficiency limitations imposed by absorption and the trade-offs between luminous and unidirectional photon sources can be understood.

The electrical conductivity of granular materials diverges when the conductivity of the constituent particles exceeds a certain threshold related to the dielectric properties of the inter-particle screening screening screen.  However, if insulating particles have a strong dielectric interaction, a new form of screening emerges, characterized by a non-standard screening length.  Researchers recently proposed an anomalous screening theory, but it had never been tested before, until researchers recently conducted an experiment involving annealed granules made of soft plastic balls.  By measuring the granule's conductivity as a function of grain size, they found it to be in perfect agreement with theoretical predictions that took into account the unique screening phenomenon, up to a critical particle size that marks the boundary between the two screening mechanisms.

This research investigates experimentally and theoretically how decorating manganese atoms onto hexagonal boron nitride affects the electronic properties of silicene. Utilizing a scanning tunneling microscope, our experiment reveals that manganese-decorated silicene is embedded within hexagonal boron nitride and possesses an increased bandgap. Comprehensive ab-initio calculations confirm that manganese decoration induces the formation of an insulating silicene monolayer, which is in line with our experimental findings.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging from extremely young, around 1-2 thousand years, to a significantly older, 10 thousand year estimate. Our study focuses on a dense gas cloud located at the center of the Sgr A East supernova remnant, aiming to determine the cloud's origin. By analyzing the carbon monoxide emission, we identify a unique spiral arm pathway that suggests the Sgr A East supernova occurred approximately 10-15 thousand years ago, along with a potential age range for the supernova of 12-17 thousand years. Our results support an older age estimate for the Sgr A East supernova, which is in line with independent Gaia observatory data suggesting that the Sgr A East supernova is significantly older than previously thought, further emphasizing the need for further investigations into the Sgr A East supernova's formation.

Oversampling, a technique used to balance sample distributions, is particularly effective in categories with fewer samples when resampling methods are employed. There are various oversampling methods that have been developed to classify supervised learning samples, particularly in imbalanced datasets. This paper focuses on the application of oversampling methods in text data sets, identifying a gap in the use of oversampling methods for natural language processing due to the uniqueness of text data. We propose three text-specific oversampling methods: combining characters, combining words, and creating text combinations, and evaluated their performance alongside existing methods in a comparative study. These methods were further adapted to enhance their distribution balance properties before applying them to the NUS7 news corpus and the IMDB dataset. We investigated the performance enhancement of the proposed distribution balance oversampling methods using various evaluation metrics, including accuracy, F1-score, Matthews correlation, and the correlation of the predicted class distribution with the original class distribution. We conducted a comprehensive comparison of the proposed methods with state-of-the-art oversampling methods using three datasets to demonstrate their efficacy in text classification. Our experiments showed that the proposed distribution balance oversampling methods are effective in improving the accuracy of text classification. We have made the source code for the proposed methods available on GitHub at https://github.com/TMJFrancis/Oversampling-for-NLP.

This study analyzes data from an online survey of 2,996 U.S. newspapers to explore the connections between COVID coverage, local case and death rates, and audience characteristics. By examining a comprehensive dataset from January 2020 to June 2021, this research quantifies COVID coverage in terms of frequency and scope, and investigates differences in coverage patterns among newspapers based on factors like region, size, and income level. The results reveal significant correlations between COVID coverage and actual cases and deaths in many U.S. counties, but also show that this connection is absent in a large number of counties, particularly those experiencing higher COVID cases and deaths. Interestingly, newspapers in higher-income areas tend to cover COVID more extensively, but there's no subsequent increase in coverage as income rises. Furthermore, this research finds that COVID coverage is more closely related to case rates at the county level than at the state level, and that newspapers in counties with younger and more educated audiences are more likely to cover COVID extensively. In terms of audience characteristics, this research finds that COVID coverage increases as audience age and income increase, but decreases as audience education increases.

The Fast Multipole Method has been the subject of research efforts for approximately three decades, and its recent adaptation for gradient-based transport schemes has sparked ongoing interest. Historically, the FMM algorithm has maintained perfect angular momentum conservation in particle scattering processes; however, with the transition to non-standard basis ordering on non-uniform grids, this property has been lost. In high-performance computational science, preserving angular momentum conservation is crucial not only for maintaining accurate results but also for ensuring code integrity and benchmark validation. This work seeks to address the loss of this essential property by investigating the underlying causes and proposing two effective solutions that involve reordering grid points and transforming non-standard velocities to maintain angular momentum conservation. Experimental evidence confirms the effectiveness of these approaches, and further development aims to incorporate these improvements into widely-used open-source coding frameworks.

Numerical calculations have been carried out for the $10\%$ level of precision in the specific case of electron-proton scattering where both the proton and electron are initially polarized, to determine how each component contributes to the total cross-section. It has been found that the proton's initial polarization contributes the majority of the time, roughly 65%, with the rest attributed to the electron's polarization. Furthermore, inside the $Q^2$-interval considered ($0.1$ -- $1.0$ GeV$^2$), the proton's polarization never actually falls below 10%. These results indicate that measuring such a cross-section could be a viable approach in confirming E-Hadron experiments' findings where the proton shows properties consistent with RHIC's data of a polarization transfer of approximately 20%.

In a scenario where a learning algorithm relies on multiple parametric experts, each with their own defined probability distribution, the task involves using a limited number of examples to make the best predictions possible. Current methods typically focus on selecting the most informative examples first, but we take a different approach by augmenting the available data with synthetic samples, ensuring all experts have sufficient information from the start. Our strategy doesn't require any prior knowledge about the experts and can be easily applied, as it relies solely on the algorithms used for sampling. We evaluate our method against established techniques on both tabular and text-based datasets, finding it results in better predictions with fewer examples on average, as well as in significantly fewer training steps overall.

A study by the ATLAS collaboration at the Large Hadron Collider, analyzing 139 fb^-1 of collision data, seeks to observe Higgs boson pairs (hh) accompanied by a vector boson (V, where V stands for W or Z or a gamma photon), compared to an embedded, predicted standard model background process (tZ). After isolating events with 2b, bh, WW, ZZ, or ττ final states, ATLAS found no significant deviations from expected values. Constraints on Higgs boson coupling modifiers, including alpha_terra, alpha_w, and alpha_z, as well as a maximum hh production cross section of 600 fb, were set through a combined effort.

We've developed a unique spin laser using sodium atoms, where the digital laser output features precise, narrow pulses at a very high repetition rate. The sodium atoms are cooled to a specific quantum state called an intersection point and then trapped using an optical lattice. When this is done, the sodium atoms are in a state of precise quantum coherence. A precise laser beam is used to transfer this coherence to a larger number of atoms, and then a second laser beam creates an interference pattern that forces the sodium atoms to release their stored energy in perfect sync. The resulting digital laser beam has a very short pulse width and can be repeated very quickly, featuring a coherence breath that is much larger than the original group of atoms. The resulting digital laser output is extremely pure, both spectrally and spatially. Our experiment has shown the feasibility of this unique method for creating precise, digital laser outputs using atomic systems.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, we show that the maximum of the absolute values of all Picard values cannot exceed the diameter of the Siegel disk, with equality occurring when the K3 surface is an elementarily finite K3 surface associated with a Hecke group. Furthermore, we examine K3 surfaces associated with classical Hecke groups and investigate the scenario where the K3 surface's Picard values are all realized as the diameters of the Siegel disks of its automorphisms.

In the context of supersymmetric models, it's argued that the neutralino could serve as a prominent component of dark matter. Given that the neutralino is a member of the third generation with significant annihilation cross-sections at MeV scales, it's plausible that the neutralino's abundance would be reduced due to self-annihilation processes occurring prior to the universe's matter-radiation equality phase. This decreased abundance is then analyzed in conjunction with X-ray observations and gamma ray data from the Fermi telescope, demonstrating that the neutralino's mass is constrained to be above 50 GeV to accommodate both phenomena simultaneously. Notably, this low upper bound stands in contrast to the 125 GeV limit set by the LHC, albeit under the conditions of a thermally suppressed self-interaction typical of supersymmetric models.

The main objective of this study is to develop an efficient method for approximating the genus of highly complex graphs with large number of edges. Although previously developed methods for obtaining a high-probability approximation within a constant factor were computationally demanding, our research proposes a more efficient technique with a faster runtime. We introduce an innovative algorithm that analyzes a given graph and determines a suitable surface on which it can be projected with the lowest possible genus, all within a polynomial time framework that adapts to the size of the input graph. This method leverages existing polynomial-time algorithms for determining tight upper bounds on the genus of a given graph. Based on this, we establish an inductive proof that our algorithm can generate an effective polynomial-time approximation scheme for graphs with a large number of edges. Our research further enhances our understanding of the computational complexity of the graph genus problem by demonstrating that it lies in the $\textbf{PL}^1$ complexity class under specific conditions. This achievement is based on a recently established approximation scheme for solving the graph genus problem.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly reducing required communication frequency. Convergence analysis and performance preservation of the method are confirmed for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, with practical applicability and efficiency further demonstrated in data-intensive scenarios.

This research focuses on identifying hate speech within Hindi and Bengali social media content, leveraging transfer learning and the versatility of neural networks. Previous studies indicated a shortage of datasets on hate speech in these languages, thus the authors developed a dataset by transcribing and annotating raw social media data for the first time. This study showcases a dataset rich in high-quality annotations and a detailed description of its creation, including considerations for maintaining users' anonymity. Moreover, the authors examine the applicability of various neural network architectures, including convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks, in hate speech detection using neural networks, and discover that transfer learning yields the greatest accuracy results. In this research, the authors apply transfer learning using pre-trained models for the English and Spanish languages, and analyze its effectiveness on the newly developed Hindi and Bengali dataset. This study aims to contribute a resourceful dataset and exploratory analysis to the field of hate speech detection in neural network-based systems.

In particle detectors with low masses, such as microbolometers, the recoil of nuclei influenced by interactions with weakly interacting massive particles can be measured. Recently, the limitations of current gas time projection chambers can be overcome using advanced technologies. A novel gas TPC employing 3D detection of ionization will have the highest sensitivity yet to nuclear recoils, utilizing the ionization signal in the gas or a noble vapor. This work presents newly proposed observables that maximize sensitivity to DM, while minimizing the impact of background events. These quantities are particularly significant as the physics of nuclear reactions and ionization change with velocity in light nuclei.

In making skilled decisions about commercial driving, certain choices like 
where to place a vehicle or when to show a promotional sign can impact 
evaluation, particularly from customers. To gain insight into how these 
decisions are experienced, we gathered expert feedback on several scenarios 
from both drivers and customers. By examining the opinions of these two 
groups - one consisting of commercial drivers and the other of potential 
customers - our research reveals the varied attention given to commercial 
driving decisions from a customer's perspective. This disparity suggests 
that commercial drivers' decisions may be influenced by how they perceive 
their work is evaluated by customers, yet their views on how the job is 
done are not universally agreed upon by customers. This brings up the 
important question of how drivers should prioritize customers' needs when 
making decisions that impact the experience, all while staying true to 
their own expertise. To address this challenge, our research proposes a 
model that integrates the opinions of both commercial drivers and 
customers to inform decision-making. This integrated model, known as the 
iChoice model, aims to create a more individualized and adaptable approach 
to navigating complex relationships between commercial drivers and 
passengers. Through this approach, both drivers and passengers can benefit 
from a more harmonious relationship, all while enhancing the overall 
experience for customers.

The Out-of-Category (OOC) challenge holds an important position within the ACMM 2022 conference programme, providing a platform for evaluation and comparison of deep learning methods for video action recognition outside of category boundaries. These boundary transgressions take the form of missing or incomplete class label information. It is worth noting that the lack of awareness on this data challenge reflects the historical precedence of the supervised learning paradigm within the video action recognition field. The OOC challenge has assembled a substantial and complex dataset comprising long-term video sequences spanning 200 classes from multiple sources. The challenge has designated two video streams and two task types for participation: binary classification against external categories and semi-supervised integration of category information. The competition attracted a substantial number of submissions from research teams, with code and model releases being mandatory for those selected as leaders in the various tracks. The evaluation outcome reveals P@1, P@5 and P@10 metrics above 0.9 for the binary classification task, alongside P@1, P@5 and P@50 metrics above 0.8 for the semi-supervised task, with code and model releases being shared by winning teams.

Random fields, especially those modeled as Gaussian fields, have become crucial in numerous scientific "inverse problems" aimed at inferring coordinates $x(u)$ from observed data $y(u)$ over a given geometric structure. The coordinate map $x(u)$ can take various forms, such as a function over time in a space with constant curvature, determined by random variables $u \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$. The goal here is to utilize the properties of their expected geometric structure when the distribution of $x(u)$ is multivariate normal and positive semi-definite matrix $\Sigma$ defines the distance and angles between tangent vectors, effectively turning $x(u)$ into a Riemannian surface. The observed data, $y(u)$, provides information on the random field's behavior over this complex geometry. The expected geometry, characterized by its curvature properties, is used to develop a divergence metric that gauges the similarity between two points. The divergence metric measures the geometric discrepancy between the standard Gaussian distribution, $\mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$, and any Gaussian distribution, $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$. The former is the standard Gaussian distribution, while the latter is the non-standard Gaussian distribution. The proposed metric measures the geometric discrepancy between the two Gaussian distributions using their expected geometric structure when the difference between their mean vectors is the random variable $x(u)$. This note is based on a lecture given at the 2018 Length Counts, Periodically event and serves as an accompanying discussion to the recording. Revisiting the scenario from film "The Usual Suspects", it demonstrates the application of the Ptolemaic twist, a concept from projective geometry. This illustrates a simple, yet engaging example of this theory in action. Additionally, the text touches on connections to Euler's work in projective geometry and the concept of cross-ratios. While the underlying analysis is novel, the conclusions drawn are primarily based on existing knowledge, with the primary goal of this work being to effectively communicate already established results to a non-expert audience.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(Z)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, we consider the distinct values $L(1,\pi)$ of the Hecke L-functions $L(s,\pi)$ corresponding to the Hecke oldforms $\pi$ and their classical analogs $F\otimes\chi$, where $\pi$ can be glued together from the spaces $S_{2k+
u}(N ackslash SL_2(Z))$ or $M_{2k+
u}(N ackslash SL_2(Z))$ for some $N\geq 1$, $0\leq 
u\leq k$, and show that the denominators of these values are uniformly bounded. This is achieved by first establishing an approximation theorem for certain linear combinations of Hecke L-functions, which generalizes and redefines the Linowitz-Conrey-Keating theorem for the case of GL_2 Hecke L-functions, and is analogous to the Bloch-Voronoi theorem for the case of elliptic L-functions.

In a study on spin current transport in graphene nanoribbons with armchair structure, where ferromagnetic gate control is employed, spin current properties are investigated in depth. A novel spin current transport theory is developed, building upon the non-equilibrium Equation-of-Motion approach, with a focus on non-magnetic, two-terminal devices using 2D graphene nanoribbons with transparent and transparent contacts. Our method is further enhanced with the inclusion of ferromagnetic gates that regulate spin current using a Landauer-Büttiker formalism, with carrier scattering addressed via Boltzmann transport. Spin current properties are examined in devices with different widths, edge potentials, and position-dependent gate control, all of which lead to distinct spin current patterns. These findings demonstrate that spin current control can be achieved in these graphene nanoribbon devices, which may have significant implications on the development of spintronics in these structures.

We derive some new, Korovkin-style theorems for weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multivariate real-valued functions. These theorems primarily involve applications of classical results from metric theory, particularly those concerning the interaction between compact sets and the convergence of sequences in complex topological spaces.

In 1972, Chvatal identified a critical value of n for infinite graphs in relation to pancyclicity, specifically that for n greater than 7, if n is sufficiently large, and for every partition of the vertices into two groups where the first group contains at least k vertices, it implies the existence of a cycle with at least k vertices entirely within the first group, this being a generalization of a result by Erdos which looked at the maximum order of the m-independent set in G. For n greater than or equal to 28, and for k greater than or equal to 3, it has been demonstrated that this critical value cannot be surpassed by anything less than k-1/5, it was also discovered that for k greater than or equal to 17, and for n greater than or equal to k, it is not possible for n-epsilon to be the independence count, it is also known that for n greater than or equal to 28, and for k greater than or equal to 17, the independence count cannot be surpassed by more than (k-1/n)+epsilon, it has also been discovered that for n greater than or equal to 28, and for k greater than or equal to 17, to get m greater than or equal to (k-1/n)+epsilon it means

This paper presents new data on a specific behavior of charged particles,
directed flow $v_1$, which has been studied in gold-gold, gold-osmium, and osmium-
osmium collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider. The results show that
particles with higher momenta exhibit negative directed flow, which aligns with
previous experiments, and that flow coefficients for gold-gold collisions are
similar to those of proton-proton collisions at similar conditions,
particularly centrality and rapidity, but with distinct differences for the
oscillation patterns. Furthermore, in both gold-gold and gold-osmium
collisions, $v_1$ shows minimal variations across particle type, indicating that
the interacting matter is behaving as a perfect fluid. The data also show that
the stringent conditions required to form this fluid state are consistent with
the established criteria derived from $v_1$ measurements. In addition, in
oscillation collisions, $v_1$ exhibits variations that could arise from
particular interactions involving baryon density, which may be manifested in
according to specific theoretical models of particle interactions.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex evolutionary problems efficiently by leveraging an adaptive algorithm that increases resolution as needed. Although this method demonstrated significant improvements, its performance was hindered by a limitation in handling high-dimensional problems. To address this limitation, the method has been combined with a new approach using sparse grids to analyze high-dimensional problems. By reorganizing the method to work directly with sparse grids, the new approach achieves improved efficiency without the need for a priori dimension reduction techniques. This method demonstrates the ability to solve difficult evolutionary problems independently without partial differential equation modeling, featuring time-varying coefficients and noisy observations. Notably, the new approach exhibits improved convergence at a comparable computational cost, surpassing the original adaptive spectral Koopman method's performance. Moreover, it allows for high-resolution solutions without the need for a large number of time steps, as well as robust convergence even with noisy data. To showcase its capabilities, the new approach successfully solves a difficult two-dimensional problem in atmospheric dynamics, accurately capturing the behavior of laminar flow in a cylindrical pipe. By using sparse grids, the method does not require a priori information about the partial cell occupancy, which is typically required by adaptive mesh refinement techniques. This makes the new approach suitable for high-resolution applications, such as modeling turbulent flow in a partial pipe. You can download the source code from github at https://github.com/qiuhisongyang/sg-ask.

The Outer Complex Scaling Method (OCSM) offers an alternative to traditional SCF methods, eliminating the need for complex arithmetic in solving for atomic or molecular orbitals when interacting with a strong, monochromatic electric field. OCSM achieves this by redefining the Hamiltonian to include a field-dependent scaling of the outer directional derivatives. The theoretical underpinnings of OCSM are explored, including a proof that scaled orbitals solve a nonlinear eigenvalue problem. A Fortran package has been developed to implement OCSM and initial results for atoms and molecules indicate its effectiveness, particularly its ability to eliminate branch cuts that often compromise linear SCF equations.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem in unbalanced transport. While this algorithm ensures the convergence of the iterations when the problem has a solution, a corresponding result for the unbalanced case has yet to be established. Specifically, under the condition that the input matrices are with strictly positive or zero rows and columns, we demonstrate that the Sinkhorn iterations converge towards a generalized solution that addresses the unbalanced problem. This finding reveals that the unbalanced Schrödinger problem admits a generalized solution in this specific context.

The combined results of three different analyses conducted by the ATLAS team at the LHC, where they examined various ranges of jet kinematics and identified different methods to measure top quark pairs, have yielded a cumulative cross-sectional measurement of top quark pairs that aligns with theoretical predictions and falls within the 78-97 percentile range of the standard model's expected outcomes. Specifically, their data analysis revealed a cross-sectional measurement of approximately 50.6 nanobarns, along with an associated uncertainty of 5.6 nanobarns, both of which were derived from combining 2.3 inverse femtobarns of LHC data collected at 5.02 TeV in 2017.

This study examines transport phenomena in a specially designed system,
specifically the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type, with coupled particles at its core.
We investigate the overall behavior of the particles as they move in parallel.
Our analysis shows that in the intermediate time frame, the particles exhibit
non-gaussian, localized behavior characterized by a key geometric property.
We provide a mathematical formula to capture this distinct feature.
Further, we investigate how particle distribution changes over time, specifically
in the late time frame, and derive an expression for this change, revealing
a return to normal geometric properties.

The conditions that need to be met for a convex function g are such that its second difference in the forward direction is given by $\Delta_2g(x)$, are provided. This leads to the identification of the necessary and sufficient conditions for the function $j_{\beta}(m+b+1, m-a)$ to be within the Janowski class. Furthermore, the study also explores the relationship between the obtained results and those for $j_{0}\{(m+b+1)(m-a)\}$.

During the pandemic, residents of highly populated urban areas in Northern Europe exhibited distinct walking pattern behaviors. Our research, which combined sensor data with demographic information from Stockholm and Copenhagen, revealed that richer populations continued to venture out, maintaining their share of urban foot traffic, whereas lower-income individuals significantly decreased their presence in public spaces, resulting in a decline in diversity of urban encounters and a disparity in foot traffic between rich and poor populations. Furthermore, contrasting pandemic-induced response behaviors existed between rich and poor individuals, including a lower usage of alternative routes by lower-income groups and an increased frequency of stay-at-home days, which ultimately led to a significant decrease in their share of urban foot traffic. Our findings suggest that the pandemic's impact on walking pattern behaviors predominantly stemmed from the socioeconomic status of individuals, resulting in a diminished diversity of urban encounters.

Accurately modeling two-phase flow in irregular porous media requires significant computational resources. To address this limitation, this research explores alternative numerical approaches that can tackle such problems more efficiently by leveraging advancements in sparse matrix computations. Specifically, this research involves partitioning the simulation domain into two sub-domains and utilizing specialized techniques, known as Facilitators, to enable simultaneous solving of these sub-domains through Newton methods. Here, the consequences of distinct ordering strategies based on these Facilitators are examined, and comparisons are made between the performance of these methods when used in conjunction with conventional time-stepping methods.

The property of chirality is prevalent across different fields, including optics, where it's utilized in various applications such as nonlinear photonics and metrology. Chiral structures in optics are characterized as lacking rotational symmetry, leading to distinct responses for left- and right-handed light propagation. However, research in optical chiral systems has primarily involved supporting counter-rotating light modes within ring resonators or vortex beams, allowing for two possible handedness configurations. We introduce a new optical device called the chiral handedness-selective (CHS) ring resonator, which is engineered to only support light with a specific handedness. By integrating this technology at the photonic quantum level, we can create a new quantum resource known as the single-handedness hybrid Josephson qubit, exhibiting exceptional properties such as fast operation speeds, high efficiency, and advanced connectivity. We demonstrate the potential of this technology by generating pure optical modes and predicting nearly limitless coherence times, paving the way for fast and reliable quantum computing applications.

We establish the gravitational limit of Liouville CFT, specifically focusing on its SU($k+1$) extension. This involves identifying the singular part of the Liouville CFT characters, including both the character $\mathcal{Y}_{\frac{2}{k+1}}$ and an alternative one, $\mathcal{Y}^*_{\frac{2}{k+1}}$. This characterization extends the prior findings of Ji and of the JT gravity gravitational limit of the Witten string. We confirm that the character $\mathcal{Y}_{\frac{2}{k+1}}$ equals the gravitational limit of the characters of free fermion parafermion $\mathcal{Y}_{\frac{\phi_0}{2}}$. We also use the duality between Liouville CFT and the non-topological $M$-matrix model to derive the gravitational limit of the $M$-matrix characters. This, in turn, enables the determination of the gravitational limit of the characters of the chiral deformed CFT previously studied by Dittes. Notably, this extends to the case where the base CFT is the free fermion CFT.

A new set of solutions is obtained for an altered warp drive model that incorporates a perfect fluid with varying pressure and density and a non-zero cosmological constant in flat spacetime. These solutions can be viewed as regular solutions in inertial frames in the context of Inverse Thin Place Shift. Notably, the embedded warp bubble's thickness remains a constant throughout space, a contrast to the classic warp drive model. The derived solutions are useful for exploring warp drive mechanics and have potential applications in astrophysics and general relativity.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing 
attention, cities like New York have experienced significant underground damage 
due to construction, resulting in substantial economic losses and potential 
danger to city residents. Maintaining these systems is extremely difficult due 
to the lack of accessible data, and existing documentations are often inaccurate 
or hard to access. With the rise of smart cities and advanced technologies like 
3D modeling and IoT, cities are looking for efficient solutions to manage and 
coordinate their underground infrastructure. To address this challenge, we 
propose the GUIDES framework, a real-time 2D/3D representation of underground 
infrastructure based on sensor data, guided by digital twins and data 
management. This framework enables the creation of underground infrastructure 
models by merging map data and sensor information through detection algorithms, 
resulting in accurate real-time representations. This approach can be applied 
for emergency response, maintenance planning, and data monitoring in various 
city applications.

To study the environment of trapped particles, we examined the spin dephasing of $^171\text{-}LB$ ions within a 2D crystal arranged in a linear chain. Our investigation revealed that the spin relaxation rate is 5 to 7 times larger than that measured by Wigner-Dyson wave function analysis. The higher relaxation rate is attributed to fluctuations in the crystal's modes. Utilizing the rates obtained from both methods, we determined the temperature of the $E\sim\sqrt{N}$ modes and the width of the motional distribution, as well as the average mode temperature. Our results indicate that the primary mechanism of mode heating is likely collision-assisted, with a corresponding rate of 0.36 s$^{-1}$.

TERS is an innovative spectroscopic technique offering precise spatial analysis at a nanoscale due to its unique setup with plasmonic nanostructures. Yet, accurately interpreting TERS spectra remains complicated because of diverse factors influencing it: a close proximity of the nanoprobe, a weak number of photons, different chemical environments, and lastly, high electromagnetic fields produced by the nanostructures themselves. We have successfully integrated electromagnetic interactions into a quantum model of TERS, enabling the simulation of experimentally measurable spectra. This approach, however, comes at the cost of computationally demanding optimization, surpassing the complexity of current quantum models used in spectroscopy. We use real-world examples to demonstrate the importance of considering plasmonic effects in TERS, with a specific focus on the variations within the same molecule influenced by the aforementioned factors. We have found that the plasmonic effects result in visible variations of the spectra within the range of a few eV, with a strong electromagnetic field being the primary cause. A detailed comparison of the simulated spectra, including the ratios of the second to the first peaks, matches the experimentally measured ones, with some exceptions likely due to the influence of the chemical and environmental effects. With this model, we perform calculations on specific molecules such as p-nitrobenzoic acid, confirming that the ratios of the second to the first peaks can be employed to estimate the distance between the nanoprobe and the sample. Furthermore, our results indicate that the ratio varies depending on the chemical environment

We conducted K-band observations of four nearby galaxies, including NGC 253, NGC 4051, NGC 6946, and IC 342, using the Sardinia Radio Telescope. The aim was to analyze the frequency and bandwidth of these observations to detect unusual magnetic microstructures or fine-scale dust structures that could influence radio continuum emission. To investigate this, we combined our data with high-resolution Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array observations, examining for correlations in emission patterns. However, our research did not reveal any statistically significant correlations between these different wavelength data sets. Consequently, we calculated the upper limit of extra thermal emission, specifically related to micrometer and submicrometer dust grain sizes, which did not exceed 10 and 5 mK respectively for all observed galaxies. These upper limits suggest the presence of a strong magnetic field, consistent with the established magnetic field strength in nearby galaxies, including magnetic fields in galaxies IC341 and NGC 253.

Ammonium sulfate, a prototypical ferroelectric and caloric material, has long been the subject of controversy regarding the origin of its entropy changes associated with ferroelectric and caloric transitions. This was addressed by combining theoretical simulations, infrared spectroscopy, and molecular terms to create comprehensive structural and energetic models of the high-symmetry and low-symmetry phases. These models enabled the calculation of phonon properties and molecular vibrations in both phases. It was discovered that the high-symmetry phase exhibits an abundance of low-frequency modes which rapidly vibrationalize upon high-low symmetry transitions. However, due to an anharmonic suppression of these modes in the low-symmetry phase, a substantial entropy increase results, mainly due to a significant number of these modes becoming degenerate. Furthermore, it was found that the entropy increase stems from a significant contribution of entropy associated with these degenerate modes. These findings highlight the importance of using accurate vibrational entropy estimates based on simulated phonons and molecular vibrations, rather than assuming ideal gas entropy, in order to understand the physical implications of the caloric effect.

In probabilistic learning, organisms gauge their environment's value-based expectations by evaluating discrepancies between forecasts and outcomes, referred to as prediction errors. Typically, optimal forecasting strategies align with these estimation outputs. However, suboptimal forecasting approaches that still allow for accurate learning outcomes, such as using different metrics for forecasting and evaluation, are often observed in various studies. Moreover, research suggests that individuals exhibit consistent preferences, known as personality traits, towards certain forecasting methods. To explain these patterns, it is proposed that midbrain areas responsible for dopamine release associate expected outcomes with both optimal and suboptimal forecasting measures, whereas the prefrontal cortex evaluates the efficacy of forecasting strategies. To investigate the relationship between suboptimal forecasting, trait-like preferences, and their neural correlates, researchers asked participants to manage risk and ambiguity in a decision-making task. Notably, participants who consistently preferred less ambiguous options over risk-prone options, and tended towards less optimal forecasting methods, showed heightened activity in brain regions associated with reward value during outcome assessments. However, these results are specific to this particular decision-making task and do not account for individual differences in personality types. Additionally, researchers found that less optimal forecasting methods and trait-like preferences are linked to weaker outcomes in life, such as lower life satisfaction and achievement. Importantly, these findings raise the hypothesis that utilizing suboptimal forecasting methods and exhibiting trait-like preferences may hinder personal growth and success.

Researchers investigate the possibility of applying complexifications to the symplectic form of a modified E8 lattice system to understand fundamental principles of quantum mechanics. This approach leads to unexpected outcomes, including the potential for accelerating quantum computations and the discovery of entangled particles. These particles could exist in a core system and be separated by complexifications. Furthermore, an investigation into the rotations of complexifications reveals the existence of highly controlled context-dependent behavior. This phenomenon raises questions about generalizing this approach to apply to all 24-dimensional spin systems.

The challenge of finding nearly adjacent data points within a certain threshold in high-dimensional datasets has far-reaching implications in various scientific and engineering disciplines, yet it remains an underexplored area in time series data. Despite existing solutions for close neighbor searching in time series under the Fr\'echet distance, all have been confined to one-dimensional time series and lack quantifiable guarantees on precision and memory storage. In our research, we present an exact and efficient algorithm for this problem in d-dimensional \mathcal{F}_k time series data, which enables us to derive tight upper and lower bounds on query time and index storage requirements. By optimizing our approach through pre-processing, we are able to achieve a logarithmic trade-off between the number of stored series and query time, thus enabling the creation of scalable and efficient search indices for multi-dimensional time series data.

The effectiveness of quantum computing relies on the processing and manipulation of precise information, but this accuracy is compromised by unavoidable distortions triggered by interactions with the surrounding environment. Since errors occur during data transmission from the quantum system, accurately decoding this information is only possible if measurements are precise, which is compromised by noise. Measuring the quantum system results in an error-deteriorated distribution of the measured property, which is corrupted by an irreparable loss of detail and the distortion of its structure due to the irreversible process of measurement itself. This paper presents an iterative technique, which utilizes Bayesian unfolding to improve the accuracy of measurement results, while also addressing the known problem involving inverse problems related to Bell measurement of multipartite quantum states using maximum likelihood methods. The proposed Bayesian unfolding approach is systematically applied to various multipartite quantum systems, including Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states of three and four qubits.

As robots increasingly interact with people in daily life, their ability to work alongside individuals as equals relies on effective communication. To achieve this, robots must be able to convey their intentions and understand the messages of those they interact with. We introduce three fundamental communication protocols - Speech, Gesture, and Teasing - that allow humans and robots to communicate through interaction. These protocols enable robots to communicate their intentions and humans can respond with relevant actions. We then extend a existing framework for telepresence to incorporate these new communication protocols. Through user testing, we gathered data on how nonverbal communication affects human-robot interaction and discovered that the Speech protocol is preferred by humans but the Gesture protocol resulted in more efficient task completion. Additionally, as users became more accustomed to the robot's communication style, the Teasing protocol led to greater engagement and improved experience. Our research lays the groundwork for developing new communication protocols and could ultimately create more harmonious human-robot interactions.

For navigation in unfamiliar environments, mobile agents require effective mapping and localization systems that combine well. Existing systems, such as those based on SLAM using pose graphs or tree data structures, have shortcomings, including computational inefficiency, localization complexity, and system rigidity. To address these issues, we present a novel mapping approach, dubbed HiTMap, which utilizes a hierarchical graph structure to represent an environment's topology. This method separates the mapping and localization processes, allowing for independent update and improved localization efficiency. Orthonormal coordinate systems are introduced in each subgraph to facilitate localization, and to ensure topological consistency, we propose a randomized algorithm that adjusts the graph structure as needed. Unlike pose graph SLAM, our system does not involve nonlinear optimization, making it suitable for real-time processing, and the structure of our graph allows for easy visualization and enhanced system usability. Compared to other methods, HiTMap demonstrates superior localization efficiency while using the same amount of map data. Experimental results using HiTMap on a mobile robot platform confirm its effectiveness in unknown environments.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with supplementary codes, which prevent interference between subgroups, has gained significant interest. Conventional inter-group complementary code sets, despite their potential, are largely ineffective in practical applications. This paper presents an innovative approach to constructing a 2-D Z-supplementary array code set based on multivariable functions. By dividing a multidimensional function region into discrete areas, unique binary two-dimensional arrays can be created. Notably, these two-dimensional arrays possess the property that, given any two distinct points with varying values, there exist at least two possible entries differing by one in both rows. Furthermore, given any two distinct column vectors, there exist two possible entries differing by one in both rows and columns. This proposed technique is versatile and enables the generation of Z-supplementary array code sets with varying sizes. Moreover, several optimal size parameters can be identified based on two variables. Examples and software-based calculations demonstrate the feasibility of constructing Z-supplementary array code sets with 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, or 512 units.

A unique four-dimensional (4D) computed tomography (CT) reconstruction model incorporating the effects of noisy sensors and varying energy levels is developed. To model the sensor noise, a special transformation is introduced that retains its low-frequency component and significantly simplifies sensor data. Subsequently, a detailed mathematical description of each other's propagation is achieved by projecting information onto a limited set of low-frequency sensor data, utilizing a limited number of energy levels, and optimizing an extended total variation regularization model. This model includes terms for similarities between consecutive frames, differences in attenuation based on material types, and the use of sensor data. An alternating projection algorithm is utilized to solve the resulting problem through split Bregman decomposition. Numerical experiments using actual data show that the method successfully neutralizes sensor noise and distinguishes between key materials. Using numerical experiments, the efficacy of the method in handling sensor noise and estimating material densities is verified.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare it to a model that accounts only for a charged surface. We demonstrate that as the gap narrows, the key characteristics of the light propagation - including frequency, intensity, and electrical properties - in the presence of both effects and in the model that accounts only for a charged surface converge towards a common value. However, the thickness of the electron spillover influences the light propagation, causing its electric component to diverge from the model that accounts only for a charged surface, even in the limit of very small gaps. Furthermore, the outcome of the model that accounts only for a charged surface depends on the choice of the wavelength used in the initial stage of the calculation and can thus be considered unreliable. This finding, alongside another discovered phenomenon where the electric component of the light propagation diverges from the model that accounts only for a charged surface, motivates the development of new, more versatile theoretical models for describing light propagation in the cross-plane of thin layers or gaps.

In a structured context like a healthcare record, finding the most relevant 'patient' when searching for a job is a challenging task, made even harder when using a database with millions of potential matches. We propose a new approach called Term Relevance Response (TRR) for Contextual Named Entity Retrieval that prioritizes relevance in a large database query. We simulate real-world scenarios within a healthcare setting and compare our TRR approach, which uses contextual information and dependent dynamic memory, against a range of baselines including full text matching and word embeddings. Our results show that by taking the context into consideration, our approach significantly improves the accuracy of entity retrieval, with an impressive 25% boost when using two sentences of contextual information. We achieve this level of accuracy with as few as 7 retrieved results from the database, which is particularly advantageous given that more options are likely to lead to information overload issues.

For analysts working with COVID-19 data, visualizing intricate time series and massive datasets can be overwhelming, necessitating both detailed and broad perspectives. Combining data from multiple sources, like daily case numbers and hospital capacity, across various geographic regions or states, creates complexity. As COVID-19 data evolves, analysts must consistently examine increasingly larger datasets over time, from daily observations to weekly or monthly totals. Nevertheless, existing visualization tools often fail to accommodate both granular and aggregated views efficiently. In response, we introduce a novel interactive framework built on fine-grained, temporally-oriented hierarchies rooted in partitioning trees. This system permits seamless transitions between perspectives, from high-detail local analyses to broader aggregated views, in sync with the underlying data sources. To enhance user experience, we also incorporate intuitive navigation features, like scalable brushes for focusing on specific time periods, region selection, and flexible querying. These capabilities enable analysts to easily explore multiple perspectives in real-time, making it simpler to identify patterns. We present a comprehensive case study on COVID-19 analysis that demonstrates the effectiveness and potential of our proposed visualization framework.

In the medical field, graph neural networks have started incorporating patient data by transforming it into a graph, where nodes represent patients and edges signify relationships. Researchers investigate how graph node similarity measures impact node representations in graph neural networks when working with healthcare data. Typically, node similarity metrics are based on a single variable or eigenvalue decomposition of the adjacency matrix, neglecting inter-relationship influences. We introduce a new node similarity measure called heterogeneous resemblance, which combines multiple nodal features, including type and quantity, with the help of real-world electronic health records and demographic data. This approach's efficacy is demonstrated through experiments on two real-world datasets.

A theoretical framework has been developed to examine the electric double layer that forms around a flexible surface in an electrolyte solution. Accounting for the ability of the solvent to polarize, the interaction between this flexible surface and the ions is modeled using a generalized Poisson-Boltzmann equation. The equation incorporates the electrostatic interaction between the different components and their respective activities. As a result, the equation is capable of being reduced to various modified versions of the Poisson-Boltzmann equation under specific assumptions, including the exclusion of ion size and the presence of ion-ion correlations. Additionally, the equation provides for the gradual transition of the ion distribution from a bulk state to one where the flexible surface is not influenced. The implications of the solvent's polarization on the ion distribution are also a product of this framework. Further analysis is provided through numerical calculations based on a couple of scenarios, including the modification of the distribution of ions near a flat surface and a charged micelle, where the polarization of the solvent is shown to influence the distribution of ions near the charged surface. The modifications caused by the solvent's polarization result in the decrease in the density of ions near the surface, with this effect being more pronounced at lower concentrations of ions. The modifications caused by the solvent's polarization are observed to reduce the pressure experienced by the surface, with this effect being more pronounced in the case of the modified Gompper model.

The growing reliance of software systems on supplementary documentation, required by law, poses challenges for developers, architects, and engineers. Documentation serves various purposes, such as documenting requirements, specifications, testing methods, and maintenance history. While these documents are essential for existing systems, they often remain inactive, unused, and ineffective in supporting development processes, as they are static and unsearchable. To rectify this issue, this research introduces a novel method to extract specifications from unstructured documents. By designating specific tags in system documentation, this method can differentiate operational documents, enabling a processor to extract and analyze the content based on these tags. Our method uses NLP to identify and understand extracted content, allowing for search and retrieval functionality. Additionally, this approach can adapt various data formats, such as HTML, XML, JSON, and documents with embedded tables, by applying a mapping that transposes structure from one format to another. To validate the efficacy of our method, we conducted experiments and case studies that demonstrated how this approach can automatically retrieve specifications from unstructured documents, facilitating the search and retrieval process.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in multi-node, multi-frequency, and multi-stream networks by utilizing collaborative network coding techniques. A scheduling-power allocation problem is formulated to optimize various energy-oriented performance metrics, utilizing different optimization techniques such as myopic and distributed algorithms with QoS guarantees. A central issue addressed in this study is the complexity associated with these optimization problems, which necessitates approximate methods like relaxations and bisection algorithms to obtain practical solutions. The study also introduces a new method of checking the feasibility of these optimizations. By utilizing numerical simulations, the performance of these algorithms is evaluated and compared under different scenarios.

The yield of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states in particular, the YSR0 state, placed exactly at the Fermi level, strongly depends on both the impurity and the substrate's characteristics. In particular, for an Mn atom positioned on a non-magnetic Nb surface, the presence of other electrons in the system causes the YSR0 state to shift away from the Fermi level, resulting in distinct YSR state energies located just above and below the Fermi level. This displacement is attributed to the exchange interaction between the Mn atom's local spin and the electrons that form the YSR states. In cases where an Mn cluster consists of more than one magnetized Mn atom, the exchange interaction between these atoms leads to a unified exchange field, which in turn causes all YSR states to shift away from the Fermi level. In such cases, the width of the exchange-spread YSR states is directly related to the magnitude of the exchange field generated by the Mn cluster. In both the case of a single Mn atom and Mn clusters, the YSR states exhibit a particular energy dispersion pattern, which is characterized by dispersion both within the same sublattice and between different sublattices, ultimately resulting in a complex set of YSR state energies. Distributions-to-distribution (DtD) scan matching is approached as an unsupervised learning problem, where various deep learning methods prioritize speed over accuracy. Nonetheless, existing techniques inherit mapping biases from their training data, resulting in inaccurate location estimates and failure to generalize. This research outlines a framework for accelerating DtD scan matching while reducing mapping biases. A novel deep learning method utilizes multiple source databases, combining individual pose estimates like an catadioptric lens, thereby minimizing localization biases. Additionally, domain-adaptive regularization techniques enable generalized learning across databases. Compared to conventional methods, our approach prioritizes speed. Anomaly detection powered by a dual-network filter identifies instances with the highest potential for biased maps, and recommended regularization strategies optimize performance across multiple source databases. This work is unique in its focus on bias mitigation, allowing localized adjustments to address specific biases, thereby enhancing overall accuracy and flexibility.

This paper aims to rectify the unconscionable disparity between the complexity and resource intensity of deep learning-based techniques. It presents an efficient, simplified method for identifying edges in satellite images, leveraging established techniques such as Canny edge detection combined with morphological operations. This approach is feasible in resource-constrained environments and offers a more transparent solution in comparison to the prescriptive deep learning model. Additionally, the paper highlights a conspicuous object in satellite images, namely an aircraft, which is shown alongside the results of our edge detection approach.

To address the non-linear aspects of XANES, researchers use simulations based on rate models of electron-surface interactions. Nevertheless, there is a lack of comprehensive theoretical framework in the existing advanced rate models. This work develops a fundamental Electron Group Model that explains XANES in a unified way, covering a wide flux range from the perturbative to the perturbative regime. By generating multi-velocity electron distributions with random trajectories that satisfy fundamental constraints, this novel model extends the conventional rate models. Electron group transitions provide the physical basis for the absorption signal's temporal structure. Numerical simulations reveal that the multi-velocity electron distribution is crucial for both XANES shape and line width. This new model is capable of simulating XANES with high flux and flux enhancement accuracy and offers valuable physical insights into target material parameters. Therefore, it is an all-encompassing theoretical tool for investigating XANES in highly flux environments.

The application of Deep Learning (DL) has significantly enhanced the performance of Software-Defined Radio (SDR) modulation recognition. Nevertheless, the vulnerability of deep learning models to malicious attacks necessitates the development of robust and resilient classification systems. This research presents an innovative solution to the problem, which involves the utilization of a Deep Neural Network (DNN) based Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) in a robust modulation recognition framework. The application of GAN in robust SDR classification achieves robustness by producing diverse examples to augment the training data, thereby incorporating a diverse set of challenges into the training set. Additionally, the application of GAN helps to mitigate the impact of adversarial attacks on the model. Experimental results confirm that the use of GAN-based data augmentation methods can improve the model's resistance to adversarial attacks. Furthermore, the robustness of the model is evaluated using three distinct metrics: the Peak Intensity (PI) of the activation functions, the L2 distance, and the Canonical Correlation Index (CCI) of the activation functions. This research employs a fundemental GAN architecture, referred to as GAN1. In order to further improve the model's resistance to adversarial attacks, two novel GAN architectures were explored. The first architecture (GAN2) employs an additional discriminator that dynamically adjusts the step size of the perturbation maps (PMs) based on an estimate of the distance of the PMs from the origin. Using a large, multi-center dataset containing MRI scans of patients with RRMS, we compared the effectiveness of two methods: training a model using data from all hospitals, and training a model for each hospital separately. While combining data from all hospitals can be beneficial, we found that it sometimes leads to overfitting. Our results indicate that training separate models for each hospital, known as hold-out cross-validation, is the most accurate approach. This is because each hospital has its own unique characteristics and characteristics of the scans can be considered as an additional feature, which was verified by analyzing the red blood cell dataset. This finding has implications for other fields where data may vary across institutions, and highlights the potential benefits of using hold-out cross-validation in such cases.

Recent breakthroughs in the study of contrast have established its significance in the theoretical coordination of perception and meaning within linguistic systems. Previous research primarily focused on the role of contrast as a means of differentiation, highlighting how various linguistic forms contrast with one another. This understanding is often applied to the limitation of possible interpretations of utterances and the facilitation of subseqeunt inferences. This study, on the other hand, is centered on the concept of contrast as a means of differentiation within the utterance itself, emphasizing the role of contrast in the generation of meaning. The perspective presented here is characterized by the incorporation of the notion of bipolar contrast, referring to the simultaneous association of a concept with two potentially contradictory characteristics. This perspective is applied to the examination of several complex areas of inquiry, including metaphoric language, the modal structure of the English past perfect and its counterparts in other languages, the modal physics of the English would and its counterparts in other languages, and the modal physics of the English volitional volitives and their counterparts in other languages.

This research introduces an innovative framework that leverages machine learning to pinpoint and quantify errors in modeling for complex systems, with a particular focus on environmental modeling. By combining numerical methods and machine learning, this approach generates a statistical model of "model error" based on real-world system behavior, where such behavior deviates from an idealized model. By constructing this "model error" probability distribution, this framework enables accurate predictions of system behavior and its associated uncertainties. As a demonstration of its potential, this research successfully applies this framework to two distinct real-world scenarios: (i) predicting water pollution and (ii) forecasting lake water levels. Both applications showcase the effectiveness of this method in identifying and rectifying modeling flaws.

The formation of massive stars is more effective in smaller, dense molecular clouds due to their lower surface density. However, it remains unclear how these clouds evolve into more massive ones before producing red supergiant stars. Observations of one such low-mass cloud, called W3-MM1, have shown a significant increase in its central radius over a 20-year period, as measured by $^{13}$CO(1-0). Data from the N$_2$H$^+$(1-1) and CS(2-1) transitions further indicate an external pressure and a mass growth rate of 5.53 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$ $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$. Furthermore, a significant increase in the gas-to-dust ratio in the central region suggests an embryonic star formation transition, while a newfound outflow indicates that star formation is approaching a critical phase. However, the cloud's central density remains stable, suggesting that overprotonation does not seem to be a key factor in the observed changes. Ultimately, the evolution of W3-MM1 may hold the key to how these massive stars come to exist.

A novel computational approach, PopSyCLE, is utilized to estimate the quantity of dark matter in the form of primordial black holes within the framework of the Kaganovich model. The program enables users to input a function representing the primordial power spectrum and generate predictions for the abundance and mass function of primordial black holes. PopSyCLE is then utilized to calculate the expected mass of a single primordial black hole that constitutes all of the dark matter, as well as the potential signal it may produce in binary mergers and the cosmic microwave background, particularly through lensing effects. The algorithm is applied to power spectra representing two scenarios: one where inflation occurs randomly with varying scales and another with inflation influenced by a particular field. The findings indicate that, depending on the power spectrum and mass of these black holes, the expected signal may emerge only after analyzing vast amounts of binary merger data or changes in the cosmic microwave background, particularly for black holes with masses between $10^{17}$ and $10^{22}$ grams.

We utilized molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the geometric disorder phase (GPD) with modulation in the direction of the director in systems consisting of rigid, wedge-shaped molecules composed of spheres where the distance between the polar head and the first edge was varied. The effects of altering the distance between the polar head and the first edge on the observed phases were examined. At a specific temperature, systems of different sizes consisting of wedge-shaped molecules with identical volumes were created to allow for comparisons between small and large molecules. The results showed that the farther the polar head was situated from the first edge, the more the director modulation spectrum frequencies differed. In systems where the polar head was close to the first edge, the resulting tetrahedral structures led to four-fold symmetry optimizations; this caused the peaks in the director modulation spectrum to appear near the corresponding wavevector that exhibited the highest symmetry optimizations frequency fluctuations. In systems, however, where the polar head was far away from the first edge, the resulting spherical volumes led to the optimizations occurring at the system's center; instead, the director modulation occurred in relation to the system's center, which caused the peaks in the director modulation spectrum to appear near specific frequencies related to the system's size. In systems, especially at large sizes consisting of wedge-shaped molecules with geographical separations far away from the polar head, the limitations in the system's size resulted in the restrictions of having four-fold symmetry optimizations; in place of the symmetry optimizations frequencies associated with the system's center. Recent breakthroughs in language modeling have led to the growth of text generation. However, generating high-quality text through transformation remains an ongoing challenge in the field. To tackle this issue, we explore adjusting existing language models to accommodate multiple tasks within a single framework. To this end, we developed PEAS, an innovative method for parameter-level adjustment that incorporates a novel adaptation technique called special token adaptation. By utilizing special tokens, which are enclosed within a model to separate inputs from different tasks, PEAS facilitates seamless multi-task training and decoupling of interference between tasks without requiring task-specific retraining. Our experiments using the MMLA dataset have shown that PEAS successfully recovers task-specific special tokens in wrapped models and achieves substantial performance improvements in text generation, with PEAS-driven wrapped models delivering 12.27% higher F1 scores than baseline models.

This paper investigates how using context in preference learning with pair-wise comparisons affects the model's ability to predict preferences for sets of items. In contrast to traditional preference learning methods that disregard context, a novel approach called Contextual Bandit Selection (CBS) utilizes context to predict preferences. A study comparing these two models revealed that a model accounting for context consistently outperformed one that does not, leading to significantly higher ranking metrics and more accurate preference predictions at smaller item counts. Moreover, the context-aware approach appeared superior across four diverse datasets. A deeper analysis of the model's performance suggested that a portion of the datasets' variation could be attributed to differing ranking types within the datasets.
